lessons.title: Pace, seam and swing

story.title: Sam from Durban learns to swing it

scenes.text: Sam, 17, in Durban, South Africa, bowls fast and straight but the ball never moves.
His coach shows him how to hold the seam upright and angled towards the slips.
In the first overs with a new ball, Sam's deliveries start curving away from the right-handers.
He takes three wickets caught behind and grins: 'It's physics, not magic!'

steps.title: The basic seam grip
steps.body:
- Hold the ball with your **index and middle fingers** either side of the seam, close together on top.
- The **thumb** rests underneath on the seam.
- Keep the ball in the **fingers, not the palm** — a gap between ball and palm.
- At release, the wrist is **behind the ball** and the seam is upright.

A ball that lands on an upright seam can **'seam'** — deviate off the pitch.

steps.title: Conventional swing
steps.body:
Swing is movement **in the air**. Bowlers keep one side of the ball shiny by polishing it (with sweat or on clothing — **saliva has been banned in international cricket since 2022**).

For **conventional swing** with a newer ball:
- The ball tends to swing **in the direction the seam points**, towards the rougher side.
- **Outswinger** (moves away from a right-hander): seam angled towards the **slips**, shiny side facing the leg side.
- **Inswinger** (moves into a right-hander): seam angled towards **fine leg**, shiny side facing the off side.

An older, scuffed ball at high pace can **reverse swing** — moving towards the shiny side.

steps.title: Variations
steps.body:
- **Yorker**: a full ball at the toes — great at the end of an innings.
- **Bouncer**: short ball rising towards head height — use sparingly; there are limits on short balls per over in playing conditions.
- **Slower ball**: changes grip (e.g., off-cutter, knuckle ball, back-of-the-hand) to deceive the batter.
- **Cutters**: fingers roll across the seam to make the ball grip and deviate off the pitch.

Master line and length first — variations work only when the stock ball is accurate.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Chasing pace by **over-striding** or bowling flat out without control.
- Holding the ball too deep in the palm → no swing, inconsistent pace.
- Using too many variations — batters line up the predictable 'surprise'.
- Bowling at full pace without a proper warm-up.

steps.title: Try this: swing experiment
steps.body: With a partner, bowl 6 balls holding the seam towards slip and 6 towards fine leg. Note which way each moved (or didn't). Swing depends on seam position, release, pace and conditions — keep a notebook of what works.

cards.back: Seam angled towards slips; shiny side on the leg side; moves away from the batter.
Seam angled towards fine leg; shiny side on the off side; moves into the batter.
Older, scuffed ball at high pace moving towards the shiny side.
Deviation off the pitch when the ball lands on an upright seam.
Full ball aimed at the batter's toes.
Fingers roll across the seam so the ball grips and deviates off the pitch.

quiz.q: For conventional swing, the ball tends to move…
options: In the direction the seam points
quiz.why: With conventional swing the ball moves the way the seam points, towards the rough side.

quiz.q: An outswinger to a right-hander has the seam angled towards…
quiz.why: For a right-hander, an outswinger moves away from the bat. The seam is angled towards the slips, and the shiny side faces the leg side.

quiz.q: Which is banned for shining the ball in international cricket?
quiz.why: The ICC banned applying saliva to shine the ball permanently in 2022. Sweat and clothing may still be used to shine it.

quiz.q: Reverse swing typically happens with…
options: An older, scuffed ball at high pace
quiz.why: Reverse swing happens when an older, scuffed ball is bowled fast. It moves the opposite way to normal swing. A brand-new ball swings conventionally.

lessons.title: Spin bowling basics: off-spin and leg-spin

scenes.text: Farhan, 11, in Hyderabad, is too small to bowl fast. He's sad at selection time.
His grandfather, a former club spinner, shows him how to flick the ball out of the back of his hand.
The ball dips, lands and spins away. The older boys in the nets are bamboozled.
Farhan is now his team's first-choice spinner. 'Size doesn't matter in spin,' his grandfather says.

steps.title: Off-spin (finger spin)
steps.body:
For a right-arm off-spinner:

- Spread the **index and middle fingers** wide across the seam, top joints on the seam.
- The **index finger** does most of the work; the thumb is lightly on the side or not used.
- At release, turn the wrist and fingers **clockwise** (like turning a door knob), so the ball spins.
- To a right-handed batter, the ball turns **from off to leg** (into the batter).

Left-arm orthodox spinners use the same finger technique and turn the ball **away** from a right-hander.

steps.title: Leg-spin (wrist spin)
steps.body:
For a right-arm leg-spinner:

- First two fingers across the seam on top; the **third (ring) finger bent along the seam** does the spinning; thumb lightly on the side.
- At release, the **wrist flicks** and the third finger rolls the ball out over the top, palm facing the batter/leg side.
- To a right-hander, the stock leg-break turns **from leg to off** (away from the batter).
- The **googly** is a leg-spinner's ball released out of the back of the hand that turns the **other way** — into the right-hander.

steps.title: Flight, drift and dip
steps.body:
Spin is not just turn:

- **Flight**: tossing the ball up on a higher arc to tempt the batter.
- **Drift**: sideways movement in the air before landing, caused by the spin.
- **Dip**: the ball dropping sooner than expected because of over-spin.
- **Pace changes** and **angle changes** (using the crease) are a spinner's best weapons.

A spinner who **spins it hard** and lands it consistently will take wickets at every level.

steps.title: Common spin mistakes
steps.body:
- **Pushing** the ball instead of spinning it — it lands flat and gets hit.
- Bowling too short (easy to pull or cut).
- Fear of being hit → bowling flat and fast. Spinners need courage to flight it.
- Not using the body: a strong pivot and follow-through help both accuracy and spin.

steps.title: Drill: spin to yourself
steps.body: Spin a ball from hand to hand while watching TV — 100 flicks a day builds finger and wrist strength. Then bowl at a single stump from half-length (about 11 yards), aiming to make the ball turn past a shoe placed in line.

activity.prompt: Match the delivery with its description (right-arm bowler, right-hand batter).
pairs: Finger spin turning from off to leg
Wrist spin turning from leg to off
Leg-spinner's ball turning into the batter
Finger spin turning away from the right-hander

quiz.q: Which finger does most of the work for an off-spinner?
quiz.why: An off-spinner uses the index finger (with the wrist) to spin the ball. The finger rolls over the ball and makes it turn from off to leg.

quiz.q: A right-arm leg-break to a right-hander turns…
quiz.why: A leg-break turns from leg to off, so for a right-hander it turns away from the batter. An off-break would turn into the batter.

quiz.q: A googly is…
options: A leg-spinner's ball that turns the other way
quiz.why: A googly is bowled by a leg-spinner with the wrist turned so that it turns the opposite way, from off to leg. The batter expects a leg-break, so it is a surprise.

quiz.q: Which is a common mistake for young spinners?
options: Pushing the ball flat instead of spinning it
quiz.why: Young spinners often push the ball flat without enough spin, so it comes at a flat pace and is easy to hit. Spinning the ball hard gets turn, dip and bounce.

lessons.title: Fielding: stopping, catching and throwing

story.title: The catch that won the final

scenes.text: Vikram, 13, from Mysuru, can't bat or bowl well enough to be a star. He's put at cover.
He spends every evening with a tennis ball against a wall: 200 catches, left hand, right hand, both.
In the final, the opposition's best batter drives hard and low. Vikram dives and holds it.
'Catches win matches,' his coach says, handing him the man-of-the-match award.

steps.title: Ready position and walking in
steps.body: As the bowler runs in, fielders in the ring **walk in** a few steps so they're moving and on the balls of their feet when the ball is hit. Knees slightly bent, hands ready, eyes on the bat.

steps.title: The long barrier
steps.body:
For a ball coming straight at you on the ground when you can't afford a miss (e.g., in the deep):

- Turn **side-on** to the ball.
- Go down on one knee so the knee touches the heel of the other foot — your leg forms a **barrier** behind your hands.
- Hands together, fingers pointing down, in front of the knee.
- Head over the ball; watch it into the hands.

In the ring, where speed matters, use an **attacking pick-up**: run in, pick up beside the leading foot, and throw in one movement.

steps.title: Catching
steps.body:
- **High catches** (above the chest): fingers pointing **up**, hands near the eyes, thumbs together; or the 'reverse cup' near the chest — follow your coach's method and practise one consistently.
- **Low catches**: fingers pointing **down**, little fingers together.
- Watch the ball all the way; **soft hands** — 'give' with the ball by drawing the hands back.
- Get your body **behind and under** the ball when you can.
- Call **'Mine!'** loudly for skied catches to avoid collisions.

steps.title: Throwing accurately
steps.body:
- Turn **side-on**, point your front shoulder and non-throwing arm at the target.
- Throw **over the top**, stepping towards the target; follow through.
- In the deep, use a **crow hop** (a skip step) to build momentum.
- Aim to reach the keeper or bowler **on the full or one bounce at bail height** over the stumps.
- Warm up your shoulder gradually before throwing hard.

steps.title: Field positions to learn
steps.body: For a right-hander, off side: **slip, gully, point, cover, extra cover, mid-off, third man, long-off**. Leg side: **fine leg, square leg, mid-wicket, mid-on, long-on, deep mid-wicket, short leg, leg slip**. Behind the bat: the **wicket-keeper**. Close positions like **silly point** and **short leg** need a helmet.

activity.prompt: Fielding drill circuit (with a tennis ball and a wall)
items: 50 two-hand catches off the wall, fingers up for high balls
50 two-hand catches, fingers down for low balls
20 one-hand catches each hand
10 long-barrier stops with a partner rolling the ball firmly
10 attacking pick-up-and-throws at a single stump
10 crow-hop throws to a partner 25–30 m away, aiming at chest height
Shoulder stretch and cool-down

quiz.q: In the long barrier, your knee should…
options: Touch the heel of the other foot to form a barrier
quiz.why: In the long barrier you kneel so that your knee touches the heel of the other foot. This closes the gap behind your hands, so the ball cannot sneak through.

quiz.q: For a low catch, fingers should point…
quiz.why: For a low catch the fingers point down, with the little fingers together. For a high catch they point up.

quiz.q: What do 'soft hands' mean?
options: Giving with the ball as it arrives
quiz.why: Soft hands means letting the hands move back with the ball as it arrives. This absorbs its pace so the ball does not bounce out.

quiz.q: Why do ring fielders walk in as the bowler runs up?
options: To be moving and ready when the ball is hit
quiz.why: Walking in as the bowler runs up gets the fielder moving on the balls of the feet. This makes the first step quicker once the ball is hit.

quiz.q: Which close position needs a helmet?
quiz.why: Close catchers such as short leg and silly point are only a few metres from the bat. They wear helmets to protect the head from hard hits.

lessons.title: Wicket-keeping basics

scenes.text: Tanvi, 12, in Nagpur, volunteers to keep when her team has nobody else.
In her first match she drops two catches by snatching at the ball.
An older keeper teaches her: 'Stay low, rise with the ball, let it come into the gloves.'
By the end of the season she has 12 dismissals, including two stumpings off the leg-spinner.

steps.title: The stance
steps.body:
- **Squat** with feet about shoulder-width apart, weight on the **balls of the feet**.
- Gloves together in front, **fingers pointing down or sideways — never straight at the ball** (to avoid finger injuries).
- Head still, eyes level, with a clear view of the ball (usually just outside off stump for a right-hander).
- Stay low until the ball pitches, then **rise with the bounce**.

steps.title: Standing back vs standing up
steps.body:
- **Fast and medium bowlers**: stand **back**, far enough that the ball reaches you around waist height after bouncing — distance depends on pace and bounce.
- **Spinners and slower bowlers**: stand **up** to the stumps (close behind them) — this stops batters leaving their crease and creates **stumping** chances.
- When standing up, a **helmet** is strongly recommended.

steps.title: Taking the ball
steps.body:
- Move **feet first** — step across with the outside leg for balls wide of off stump, so the body stays behind the ball.
- Watch the ball **into the gloves**; let the hands 'give' back towards the body.
- For a stumping, take the ball and bring the gloves **straight to the stumps** in one smooth move — don't swing wide.
- Keep the gloves together when possible, opening them like a bowl.

steps.title: Common keeping mistakes and injuries
steps.body:
- **Snatching** at the ball → drops and bruised hands.
- **Fingers pointing at the ball** → broken or dislocated fingers.
- **Standing up too soon** → you can't see the ball.
- Keepers squat hundreds of times a day — strengthen your legs and hips and warm up the knees and hips before play.

steps.title: Drill: wall keeping
steps.body: Stand 3–4 m from a wall in your stance. A partner behind you throws a tennis ball at the wall; you rise and take it. Progress to taking balls wide on both sides, using footwork. 3 sets of 20.

items.back: Down or sideways — never directly at the ball.

items.front: When do you rise from the squat?
items.back: With the bounce of the ball, after it pitches.

items.front: Stand up or back to a spinner?
items.back: Up to the stumps — it creates stumping chances.

items.front: How to take a wide ball outside off?
items.back: Step across with the outside leg; keep the body behind the ball.
Wear a helmet with a grille.

quiz.q: When should a keeper rise from the squat?
options: With the bounce of the ball
quiz.why: The keeper stays low and rises with the bounce of the ball. This keeps the eyes level with the ball and the hands soft as they take it.

quiz.q: Which bowlers does the keeper usually stand up to?
quiz.why: Keepers stand up to the stumps for spinners and slower bowlers, because the ball arrives slowly. This gives chances of stumping. For fast bowlers they stand back.

quiz.q: Why shouldn't fingers point at the ball?
quiz.why: Fingers pointing at the ball can be jammed or broken if it hits the tips. Pointing them down or up so the ball hits the palms is safer.

quiz.q: A common mistake that causes drops is…
options: Watching the ball into the gloves
quiz.why: Snatching at the ball makes the hands hard, so the ball bounces out. Soft hands, good footwork and watching the ball into the gloves prevent drops.

questions.q: Which delivery moves away from a right-handed batter in the air?
questions.why: An outswinger moves away from a right-handed batter in the air. An inswinger moves in towards the batter, and a yorker is about length, not swing.

questions.q: Which fielder may wear gloves?
questions.why: Only the wicket-keeper may wear gloves among the fielders. Other fielders, like the bowler and slips, may not.

questions.q: A ball aimed at the toes is a…
questions.why: A ball aimed at the toes is a yorker. A bouncer is short, and a googly is a spinner's delivery.

questions.q: For high catches, fingers generally point…
questions.why: For high catches the fingers point up, with the hands in front of the chest or face, so the ball cannot go through them. Low catches use fingers pointing down.

questions.q: A right-arm off-break to a right-hander turns…
questions.why: An off-break turns from off to leg, so for a right-hander it turns into the batter. A leg-break turns away.

questions.q: The long barrier is used to…
options: Stop the ball safely in the deep
questions.why: The long barrier is a safe way to stop a ball in the deep. You kneel with the knee behind the heel of the other foot, so the ball cannot get past your body.

questions.q: What is the ICC tolerance for elbow extension?
questions.why: The ICC allows up to 15° of elbow extension in a legal bowling action. A bigger bend or straightening makes it a suspect action.

questions.q: Which back-foot rule applies to a legal delivery?
options: Must land within and not touching the return crease
questions.why: A bowler's back foot must land inside the return crease and must not touch it. If it does, the umpire calls a no-ball.

questions.q: Where should a keeper stand to a spinner?
questions.why: Against spinners the keeper stands up to the stumps. This puts the keeper close to take the ball and be ready to stump, and the slow pace makes it safe.

questions.q: A young fast bowler with a mixed action is most at risk of…
questions.why: A mixed action twists the back a lot while bowling. In young fast bowlers this is linked to stress injuries of the lower back, not to wrist or ankle problems.

questions.q: With conventional swing and the shiny side facing the off side, the seam angled to fine leg, the ball should…
questions.why: With the seam angled towards fine leg and the shiny side facing the off side, the ball swings in towards a right-handed batter. This is the inswinger set-up; for an outswinger the seam points to the slips.

questions.q: What makes the 'corridor of uncertainty' effective?
options: The batter is unsure whether to play or leave
questions.why: A good length just outside off stump leaves the batter unsure whether to play or leave. This doubt is why it is called the corridor of uncertainty.

questions.q: Which describes drift?
options: Sideways movement in the air caused by spin
questions.why: Drift is sideways movement of the ball in the air caused by spin, before it pitches. It is different from turn, which happens after the ball bounces.

questions.q: Reverse swing generally moves the ball…
questions.why: Reverse swing moves the ball towards the shiny side, the opposite of conventional swing, which moves towards the rough side. It happens with an old, scuffed ball at pace.

courses.title: The complete cricketer: fitness, mental game and the pathway in India
courses.summary: How cricketers train their bodies, stay safe in heat, build a strong mind, and how the pathway from school and club cricket to district, state and beyond generally works in India — plus how to avoid fake 'selection' scams.
outcomes: Learners can plan a weekly cricket-fitness routine safely
Learners can prevent and recognise heat illness
Learners can use a between-ball routine and process goals
Learners can describe the general pathway from school/club to district and state cricket in India
Learners can spot red flags in academies or 'trial' offers

lessons.title: Fitness for cricketers

scenes.text: Kiran, 16, from Ranchi, is a talented batter but tires badly after 30 overs in the field.
At the state camp, the trainer explains that fitness tests are now part of selection at many levels.
Kiran follows a simple plan: sprints, agility, strength twice a week and proper sleep.
Three months later he's running quicker twos and his last 10 overs are as sharp as his first 10.

steps.title: Before you begin
steps.body: This is general education, not medical advice. **Consult a doctor before starting if you have a heart condition, high blood pressure, diabetes, asthma, a joint or back problem, or are recovering from injury.** Young players should train under a qualified coach. Stop if you feel chest pain, faintness or sharp pain; in an emergency call **112**.

steps.title: What cricket demands
steps.body:
Cricket is a game of **repeated short bursts**: sprinting between wickets, chasing to the boundary, bowling spells, diving, throwing — with recovery in between, often for hours in the heat.

So cricketers need:
- **Speed and acceleration** (first 5–10 m).
- **Agility** (turning, changing direction).
- **Repeated-sprint endurance**.
- **Strength and power** in legs, hips, core and upper body.
- **Shoulder and core robustness** to stay injury-free.
- **Flexibility and mobility** in hips, hamstrings and thoracic spine.

Some teams use the **Yo-Yo intermittent recovery test** to measure repeated running fitness.

steps.title: A sample week for a 15–17-year-old (in season)
steps.body:
- **Mon**: Nets + 6×20 m sprints (full recovery) + core (plank, side plank, dead bug).
- **Tue**: Strength (squat, lunge, push-up, row, hip hinge — technique first) 30–40 min.
- **Wed**: Nets + agility (cone drills, 'turn and run' between wickets).
- **Thu**: Rest or light mobility/yoga.
- **Fri**: Strength + shoulder care (band rotations, wall slides).
- **Sat/Sun**: Matches; light recovery jog and stretch after.

Adjust to your coach's plan. Younger players (under 14) should focus on fun movement skills, bodyweight exercises and lots of different sports.

steps.title: Recovery is training too
steps.body:
- **Sleep**: teenagers generally need 8–10 hours a night.
- **Eat** regular meals with carbohydrate, protein and vegetables; a snack after training.
- **Hydrate** before, during and after (next lesson covers heat).
- **Monitor workload**: sudden jumps in bowling or training load raise injury risk. Increase gradually.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Copying a professional's gym routine at 13.
- Lifting heavy with poor form to 'get big'.
- Skipping warm-ups before nets.
- Taking supplements without advice — some contain banned substances (see the nutrition course).

activity.prompt: Cricket fitness circuit (bodyweight, 25 minutes). Warm up first.
items: Warm-up: 5 min jog + leg swings, hip circles, arm circles
6 × 20 m sprints, walk back recovery
3 × 'run a three' between two cones 20 m apart (practise turns low and fast)
3 × 10 bodyweight squats with good form
3 × 8 lunges each leg
3 × 30-second plank and 20-second side plank each side
2 × 10 band or towel shoulder rotations
Cool-down: walk 3 min, stretch hamstrings, hips, shoulders

quiz.q: Cricket mostly involves…
quiz.why: Cricket has repeated short bursts like sprints, throws and bowling, with rest in between. It is not constant running like a marathon.

quiz.q: A key cause of injury in young bowlers is…
quiz.why: Young bowlers get hurt when workload jumps suddenly. Gradual increases give the body time to adapt, so sudden spikes are the risk.

quiz.q: How much sleep do teenagers generally need?
quiz.why: Teenagers generally need 8–10 hours of sleep. Sleep helps recovery, growth and concentration.

quiz.q: What should under-14 players focus on?
options: Fun movement skills, bodyweight work and many sports
quiz.why: Under-14 players should build broad athletic skills: fun movement, bodyweight exercises and playing many sports. Heavy weights, supplements or only bowling are not suitable at this age.

lessons.title: Playing in the heat: hydration and heat illness

scenes.text: It's 41°C at an under-16 match in Nagpur in April. Rahul has been fielding for three hours.
He feels dizzy, has a headache and stops sweating. He becomes confused about the score.
His coach recognises danger: they move him to shade, cool him with water and ice, and call 112.
Doctors say fast cooling made a big difference. The academy now plans drinks breaks and shade for every match.

steps.title: Why the heat matters
steps.body: In hot, humid weather your body cools itself by sweating. You can lose a lot of fluid and salt in a long session. Even modest dehydration can reduce concentration, decision-making and skill — and severe heat can be dangerous.

steps.title: A simple hydration plan
steps.body:
- **Before**: drink regularly through the day; arrive hydrated (pale-yellow urine is a rough guide).
- **During**: sip at every drinks break and between overs when possible — don't wait to be very thirsty.
- **After**: rehydrate with water and food; in long, sweaty sessions an **ORS** or a drink with some salt helps replace losses.
- Wear a **hat, sunscreen and light, breathable clothing**; rest in the shade.
- Don't force huge amounts of plain water — over-drinking can also be harmful.

steps.title: Know the warning signs
steps.body:
**Heat exhaustion**: heavy sweating, tiredness, headache, dizziness, nausea, cramps. → Stop, move to shade, cool down, sip fluids. If not improving within about 30 minutes, get medical help.

**Heat stroke** (an emergency): very high body temperature, **confusion, strange behaviour, collapse, fits**, skin may be hot (sweating may or may not have stopped). → **Call 112**, move to shade, **cool rapidly** (cold water, ice packs to neck/armpits/groin, fanning) while waiting. Don't give drinks if they can't swallow safely.

steps.title: Smart habits for Indian summers
steps.body:
- Schedule hard training early morning or late afternoon.
- Acclimatise over 1–2 weeks when the heat rises: shorter sessions first.
- Buddy system: team-mates watch each other for warning signs.
- Weigh yourself before and after a long session: each kg lost is roughly a litre of fluid to replace gradually.

a.text: You're captain in a 40°C match. Your fielder at fine leg looks unsteady and says he has a headache. What do you do first?

choices.label: Tell him to keep going till the drinks break
choices.feedback: Waiting can let things get worse quickly.

choices.label: Stop play, bring him off into the shade and tell the coach
choices.feedback: Right — act early.

b.text: Two overs later he collapses and seems confused. Now what?

choices.label: Call 112, move him to shade, cool him rapidly with water and ice
choices.feedback: Correct emergency response for suspected heat stroke.

c.text: In the shade he is sweating a lot but can talk clearly. What next?

choices.label: Cool him, give sips of water/ORS, rest, and monitor; get medical help if not better in about 30 min or he gets confused
choices.feedback: Good management of likely heat exhaustion.

choices.label: Give him an energy drink and send him back out
choices.feedback: Sending him back too soon is risky.

end1.text: He recovers. You arrange extra drinks breaks for everyone. Great leadership.

end2.text: Rapid cooling and calling 112 are exactly right. Next time, act at the first warning sign.

quiz.q: Confusion and collapse in the heat suggest…
quiz.why: Confusion or collapse in the heat means the brain is affected, which is a sign of heat stroke. This is an emergency: call 112 and cool the person quickly.

quiz.q: A rough guide that you're hydrated is…
quiz.why: Pale-yellow urine is a simple sign of being well hydrated. Dark urine means you need more fluid, and being very thirsty means you are already behind.

quiz.q: Each kg lost during a session is roughly…
quiz.why: During exercise, weight lost is mostly water, so each 1 kg lost is roughly 1 litre of fluid. It is not fat loss.

quiz.q: Which is a smart summer habit?
quiz.why: Acclimatising gradually over 1–2 weeks helps the body cope with heat. Training hardest at 1 pm, avoiding shade or waiting to drink would raise the risk of heat illness.

sources: WHO guidance on heat and health

lessons.title: The mental game: routines, focus and bouncing back

scenes.text: Zara, 15, a Mumbai opener, gets out first ball in an important match and cries in the dressing room.
Her coach doesn't talk about technique. She asks, 'What were you thinking before that ball?' 'That I mustn't fail,' says Zara.
They build a simple routine for every ball: breathe, look at the bat, a trigger word — 'Watch' — then focus.
Next match she scores 47. 'I didn't think about the score at all. Just one ball at a time.'

steps.title: Between-ball routines
steps.body:
A cricket ball takes under a second to reach you, but there are ~30 seconds between balls. What you do with that time matters.

A simple batting routine:
1. **Switch off**: walk towards square leg, relax your grip, look at something neutral.
2. **Review quickly**: 'Was that good? Fine. Next.'
3. **Breathe**: one slow breath out.
4. **Switch on**: take stance, a trigger word ('Watch', 'Ball'), eyes on the bowler's hand.

Bowlers can do the same at the top of their run-up: plan the ball, picture it, breathe, go.

steps.title: Process goals beat outcome goals
steps.body:
- **Outcome goal**: 'Score 50', 'Take 3 wickets' — you don't fully control these.
- **Process goal**: 'Watch the ball out of the hand', 'Leave well outside off', 'Hit the top of off stump' — you control these.

Focus on processes during play; the outcomes follow more often.

steps.title: Self-talk and handling failure
steps.body:
- Replace 'Don't get out' (which puts 'getting out' in your head) with **'Watch the ball'**.
- After a mistake, use a **reset**: a breath, a word, a physical action (adjusting gloves).
- Remember cricket's maths: even great batters fail often. Judge yourself over a season, not one innings.
- Keep a **cricket diary**: one thing that went well, one thing to work on, after each game.

steps.title: When to talk to someone
steps.body: Pressure from selection, parents or social media can feel heavy. If worry affects your sleep, eating or enjoyment for weeks, talk to a trusted adult or coach. In India, **Tele-MANAS (14416)** offers free mental-health support.

activity.label: Pre-ball reset: breathe in 4, hold 2, out 6. Use it before every ball in the nets this week.

quiz.q: Which is a process goal?
options: Watch the ball out of the bowler's hand
quiz.why: A process goal is an action you control, like watching the ball out of the bowler's hand. Winning, scoring a century or being selected depend on other things too.

quiz.q: Why say 'Watch the ball' rather than 'Don't get out'?
options: It focuses on what to do, not what to avoid
quiz.why: The mind follows instructions. 'Watch the ball' tells you what to do, while 'Don't get out' focuses on what to avoid and can make you tense.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of 'switching off' between balls?
options: To rest the mind so you can fully focus for the next ball
quiz.why: Nobody can concentrate intensely for hours; routines help you switch on when it counts.

quiz.q: Which Indian helpline offers free mental-health support?
quiz.why: Tele-MANAS is India's free mental-health helpline at 14416. 1098 is Childline, 100 is the police and 1912 is not a mental-health line.

lessons.title: The pathway in India: school, club, district, state and beyond

story.title: Pooja's road from a small town

scenes.text: Pooja, 13, from a small town in Haryana, plays with boys in the local maidan and wants to play for India.
Her PE teacher enters her school in inter-school matches and tells her about the district association's women's trials.
Her father collects her birth certificate and school records for age verification, and they register properly.
A man offers a 'guaranteed state selection' for ₹1.5 lakh. Her coach says: real selection is never sold. They walk away.
Two seasons of hard work later, Pooja is picked for her state's under-age squad.

steps.title: The general ladder
steps.body:
Details differ by state and change over time, but generally in India:

1. **School and local cricket**: inter-school tournaments, school games (including the School Games Federation of India events), local leagues.
2. **Clubs and academies**: regular coaching and matches in leagues run or recognised by the local/district association.
3. **District association**: holds **trials and age-group selections** (e.g., under-14, under-16, under-19) and inter-district tournaments.
4. **State association** (affiliated to the **BCCI**): picks state age-group and senior teams for national domestic tournaments.
5. **Zonal / national camps, India A and India teams** — for the very best performers.

Women's cricket has its own age-group and senior domestic tournaments, and professional leagues like the WPL.

steps.title: Some BCCI domestic tournaments
steps.body:
- **Ranji Trophy**: senior men's multi-day (first-class).
- **Vijay Hazare Trophy**: senior men's one-day.
- **Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy**: senior men's T20.
- **Cooch Behar Trophy** (U-19 multi-day) and **Vinoo Mankad Trophy** (U-19 one-day).
- **Vijay Merchant Trophy**: U-16.

Tournament formats and age limits can change; always check your state association's current notices.

steps.title: Practical steps
steps.body:
- **Register** with a club or academy affiliated to your district association.
- Keep **age documents** ready (birth certificate, school records). Age-group cricket requires age verification; age fraud can bring long bans.
- Watch for **trial notices** on official association websites and notice boards.
- Build a **record**: scorecards from recognised matches matter more than videos.
- Keep up your **studies** — very few players become professionals, and many coaches, physios, analysts, umpires and scorers also work in cricket. Coaching qualifications (e.g., NIS or board coaching courses) open careers too.

steps.title: Red flags: selection scams
steps.body:
- Anyone promising **guaranteed selection** for a state team or an IPL/WPL franchise for money.
- 'Trials' with high fees and no link to an official association.
- Pressure to pay quickly in cash, or to hide things from parents.
- Requests to change or 'adjust' age documents.

Genuine selection is based on performance in recognised cricket. If something feels wrong, check directly with the district or state association, and talk to your parents and coach.

a.text: A message arrives: 'IPL franchise talent hunt! Pay ₹50,000 registration for a guaranteed spot in the final trial.' What do you do?

choices.label: Pay quickly before spots run out
choices.feedback: Urgency and guaranteed spots are classic scam signs.

choices.label: Show your coach and parents and check official sources
choices.feedback: Smart and safe.

b.text: After paying, the number stops answering. What now?

choices.label: Report it: tell parents, keep screenshots, report to the cybercrime helpline 1930 / police
choices.feedback: Reporting quickly helps and may stop others being cheated.

c.text: Your coach finds no such trial on any official website. Your next step?

choices.label: Ignore it and focus on the district association's real trials
choices.feedback: Exactly — performance in recognised cricket is the real route.

choices.label: Pay anyway, just in case
choices.feedback: 'Just in case' is how scams win.

end1.text: You train hard, register with your district, and get noticed in recognised matches. That's the real pathway.

end2.text: A painful lesson, but reporting is right. Real trials never sell guaranteed places.

quiz.q: Which body do state cricket associations generally affiliate to in India?
quiz.why: State cricket associations are members or affiliates of the BCCI, the national board. The ICC is the world body, and the AIFF governs football.

quiz.q: The Ranji Trophy is…
quiz.why: The Ranji Trophy is India's premier first-class competition. It is for senior men's teams and is played over multiple days.

quiz.q: Which is a red flag?
options: A coach asking for your scorecards
A promise of guaranteed selection for money
A free district trial notice on the association website
quiz.why: Genuine selection is based on ability and cannot be bought. A promise of guaranteed selection for money is a warning sign of a scam.

quiz.q: Why keep age documents ready?
quiz.why: Age-group cricket needs age verification so that everyone plays at the right level. Age fraud can lead to bans, so keep your documents ready.

quiz.q: Which statement about careers in cricket is true?
options: Coaching, physiotherapy, analysis, umpiring and scoring are also careers
quiz.why: Cricket offers many careers besides playing, such as coaching, physiotherapy, analysis, umpiring and scoring. Studies still matter, and not only IPL players earn.

questions.q: Which describes cricket's physical demands?
questions.why: Cricket involves repeated short bursts of sprinting, throwing and bowling with recovery in between. It is not steady marathon pace.

questions.q: Which number is India's all-emergency number?
questions.why: 112 is India's single all-emergency number. 1098 is Childline and 14416 is the mental-health helpline.

questions.q: Which is a process goal for a bowler?
options: Hit a good length on off stump
questions.why: A process goal is something you control, like hitting a good length on off stump. Taking wickets or winning the series depends on other things as well.

questions.q: First aid for suspected heat stroke includes…
questions.why: For suspected heat stroke, cool the person quickly and call 112. Running it off or a hot drink would make things worse.

questions.q: The Vijay Hazare Trophy is a…
questions.why: The Vijay Hazare Trophy is India's senior men's domestic one-day tournament. It is not a Test series or an under-16 event.

questions.q: Which is a safer way to increase bowling workload?
questions.why: Increasing bowling workload gradually gives the body time to adapt. Doubling it in a week is a sudden jump that raises injury risk.

questions.q: A between-ball routine mainly helps you…
options: Switch off and then fully switch on for each ball
questions.why: A between-ball routine lets the batter relax and then focus fully for each ball. This manages attention across a long innings.

questions.q: Which tournament is U-19 one-day?
questions.why: The Vinoo Mankad Trophy is the Indian under-19 one-day tournament. The Ranji Trophy is first-class, and the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy is T20.

questions.q: A player loses 1.5 kg in a session. Roughly how much fluid lost?
questions.why: Body weight lost in exercise is mostly water, about 1 litre per kg. So 1.5 kg lost is roughly 1.5 litres of fluid to replace.

questions.q: Which sign best separates heat stroke from heat exhaustion?
questions.why: In heat stroke the brain is affected, so confusion or altered behaviour appears. Sweating and thirst can occur in simple heat exhaustion too, so they do not tell them apart.

questions.q: An academy says it can 'adjust' your age on documents to play U-16. You should…
options: Refuse — age fraud can bring bans
questions.why: Changing documents to fake age is age fraud. It is cheating and can lead to bans that can end a career, so refuse.

questions.q: A batter replaces the thought 'Don't nick it' with 'Watch, leave, play late'. This is an example of…
questions.why: Replacing a negative thought with a task cue such as 'Watch, leave, play late' is instructional self-talk. It points attention to what to do next.

questions.q: Which statement about the Indian cricket pathway is most accurate?
options: One fixed national system identical in every state
A general ladder of school/club → district → state (BCCI-affiliated) → national, with details varying by state
questions.why: The general ladder runs from school or club to district, then state (BCCI-affiliated), then national, but the details vary between states. It is not one fixed system in every state, and social media does not select players.

lessons.title: How much activity do we need? (WHO guidelines)

scenes.text: The Iyer family in Chennai — dad Ganesh (45, desk job), mum Lata (42), Meenu (14) and grandma Kamala (70) — realise none of them moves much.
Meenu finds the WHO activity guidelines for a school project and makes a chart for each person.
They start evening walks, Meenu joins the school football club, grandma does balance exercises with a chair.
Three months later, everyone sleeps better and grandma says climbing stairs feels easier.

steps.title: Safety first
steps.body:
This is general education, not medical advice. **Consult a doctor before starting if you have a heart condition, high blood pressure, diabetes, asthma, a joint or back problem, are pregnant, or are recovering from an injury or illness.**

Stop at once and seek help if you feel chest pain, faintness, unusual breathlessness, or sharp pain. In an emergency in India call **112**.

steps.title: Children and teens (5–17 years)
steps.body:
WHO (2020) recommends:

- An **average of at least 60 minutes a day** of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, mostly aerobic (running, cycling, sports, active play).
- **Vigorous** activities and activities that **strengthen muscle and bone** on at least **3 days a week**.
- **Limit sedentary time**, especially recreational screen time.

steps.title: Adults (18–64 years)
steps.body:
- At least **150–300 minutes a week of moderate** aerobic activity (e.g., brisk walking), **or 75–150 minutes of vigorous** activity (e.g., running), or a mix.
- **Muscle-strengthening** activities involving all major muscle groups on **2 or more days a week**.
- Reduce sitting; **some activity is better than none** — and more brings extra benefits.

steps.title: Older adults (65+) and the very young
steps.body:
- **65+**: the adult recommendations **plus** varied activities that emphasise **balance and strength** on **3 or more days a week**, to improve function and prevent falls.
- **Under-5s** (WHO 2019): lots of active play through the day — for 3–4-year-olds at least 180 minutes of varied activity, including at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous; babies should have floor-based play and tummy time.

steps.title: Worked example: hitting 150 minutes
steps.body: Ganesh walks briskly 30 minutes on 5 weekdays = **150 minutes** of moderate activity. He adds 2 short strength sessions (20 minutes each) at home. Target met. Lata prefers jogging: 3 × 25 minutes = **75 minutes** of vigorous activity — also meets the guideline.

steps.title: What counts as moderate or vigorous?
steps.body:
- **Moderate**: you breathe faster and feel warmer but **can still talk** (not sing) — brisk walking, easy cycling, dancing, gardening.
- **Vigorous**: you **can only say a few words** before needing a breath — running, fast cycling, competitive sports, skipping.

Try this: tomorrow, use the talk test during your walk and see whether it's moderate.

activity.label: Your weekly minutes of moderate activity (adult)

bands.text: No activity yet. Start small: a 10-minute walk after meals counts.
Some activity — great start! Every extra 10 minutes helps. Build towards 150.
You meet the WHO guideline (150–300 min). Add strength 2×/week.
Above 300 minutes — additional benefits. Make sure you recover and sleep well.

quiz.q: How much activity does WHO recommend for 5–17-year-olds?
options: An average of at least 60 minutes a day of moderate-to-vigorous activity
quiz.why: WHO recommends that children and adolescents aged 5–17 get an average of at least 60 minutes a day of moderate-to-vigorous activity. Much less would not give the same health benefit.

quiz.q: Adults should do muscle-strengthening on at least…
quiz.why: Adults should do muscle-strengthening activities on 2 or more days a week. These work all the main muscle groups.

quiz.q: 75 minutes of vigorous activity is roughly equivalent to…
quiz.why: Vigorous activity counts roughly double moderate activity. So 75 minutes of vigorous activity is about the same as 150 minutes of moderate activity.

quiz.q: What extra do older adults need?
options: Balance and strength activities 3+ days a week
quiz.why: Older adults should add balance and strength activities on 3 or more days a week. This kind of mixed activity helps prevent falls.

quiz.q: In the talk test, moderate activity means…
options: You can talk but not sing
quiz.why: The talk test: at moderate intensity you can talk but not sing. If you can sing, it is too easy, and if you cannot say more than a few words, it is vigorous.

sources: WHO Guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour (2020)

lessons.title: Warm-up and cool-down done right

scenes.text: Rahul, 28, a software engineer in Gurugram, rushes from office to weekend football with no warm-up.
Ten minutes in, he sprints and feels a sharp pain at the back of his thigh. Three weeks out.
His physio, Dr. Mehta, gives him a 10-minute warm-up routine.
He hasn't been injured since — and he plays better in the first ten minutes.

steps.title: Why warm up?
steps.body: A good warm-up **raises body and muscle temperature**, increases heart rate and blood flow, improves joint range of motion and 'switches on' the nervous system. It prepares you physically and mentally, and structured warm-ups (like FIFA 11+ in football) have been shown to reduce injuries.

steps.title: The RAMP framework
steps.body:
- **R — Raise**: 3–5 minutes of easy movement to raise heart rate and temperature (jog, skipping, cycling).
- **A — Activate**: wake up key muscles — glute bridges, band walks, planks.
- **M — Mobilise**: dynamic movements through range — leg swings, walking lunges with a twist, arm circles, inchworms.
- **P — Potentiate**: gradually build to the intensity of your session — strides, jumps, sport-specific drills.

Total: about **8–15 minutes**.

steps.title: Static stretching: before or after?
steps.body: Long static stretches (holding a stretch for a minute or more) right before explosive activity can slightly reduce power and speed for a short time. So before sport, prefer **dynamic** movements. Short static holds are fine if followed by dynamic work. Save longer **static stretching** for the **cool-down** or a separate flexibility session.

steps.title: The cool-down
steps.body:
- 3–5 minutes of easy movement (walk, slow jog) to bring heart rate down gradually.
- Gentle **static stretches** for the muscles you used: 20–30 seconds each, no bouncing, no pain.
- Rehydrate and refuel.

A cool-down won't prevent next-day soreness completely, but it helps you relax and recover, and is a good time to improve flexibility.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Skipping the warm-up 'to save time'.
- Going straight into sprints or heavy lifts.
- Bouncing in stretches (ballistic stretching) without training.
- Stretching into pain — mild tension is enough.

activity.prompt: Order the RAMP warm-up correctly.
items: Raise: easy jog or skipping for 3–5 minutes
Activate: glute bridges and band walks
Mobilise: leg swings, walking lunges, arm circles
Potentiate: build-up strides and sport-specific drills
Start the main session

quiz.q: What does the 'R' in RAMP stand for?
quiz.why: RAMP stands for Raise, Activate, Mobilise, Potentiate. The R is Raise: raise heart rate, body temperature and breathing with easy movement.

quiz.q: Before explosive sport, which stretching is preferred?
quiz.why: Before explosive sport, dynamic movements like leg swings and skips prepare the muscles without reducing power. Long static holds can slightly reduce power.

quiz.q: How long might a typical warm-up take?
quiz.why: A typical warm-up takes about 8–15 minutes. That is enough to raise heart rate and prepare the joints and muscles, without causing tiredness.

quiz.q: A cool-down mainly helps you…
options: Bring heart rate down gradually and relax; good time for static stretching
quiz.why: A cool-down brings your heart rate down gradually and helps you relax. It is also a good time for static stretching. It does not burn extra fat or fully prevent soreness.

lessons.title: Cardio: heart rate, intensity and building endurance

scenes.text: Fatima, 35, a teacher in Lucknow, signs up for a 5 km charity run but has never run before.
She starts with walk–run intervals: 1 minute jog, 2 minutes walk.
Every week she runs a little more. She uses the talk test to stay comfortable.
Eight weeks later she runs the whole 5 km, smiling.

steps.title: What cardio does
steps.body: Aerobic ('cardio') exercise uses large muscle groups rhythmically for a sustained time: walking, running, cycling, swimming, dancing, skipping. Regular cardio strengthens the heart and lungs, helps control blood pressure, blood sugar and weight, improves mood and sleep, and lowers the risk of many chronic diseases.

steps.title: Measuring intensity
steps.body:
- **Talk test**: moderate = can talk, not sing; vigorous = only a few words.
- **RPE (rating of perceived exertion)** on 0–10: about **3–4** moderate, **5–6** hard, **7–8** very hard.
- **Heart rate**: a rough estimate of maximum heart rate is **220 − age** (individuals can differ by 10 beats or more). Moderate is roughly 64–76% of max; vigorous about 77–95%.

Some medicines (e.g., beta-blockers) lower heart rate — use RPE/talk test instead.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Fatima is 35. Estimated max HR = 220 − 35 = **185 bpm**. Moderate zone ≈ 0.64 × 185 to 0.76 × 185 ≈ **118 to 141 bpm**. She checks her pulse or watch: 130 bpm while jogging — moderate. Remember it's an estimate.

steps.title: Building endurance: walk–run plan
steps.body:
- Week 1–2: 6 × (1 min jog + 2 min walk), 3 times a week.
- Week 3–4: 5 × (2 min jog + 1 min walk).
- Week 5–6: 3 × (5 min jog + 1 min walk).
- Week 7–8: 20–30 min continuous easy jog.

Repeat a week if it felt too hard. Consistency beats intensity.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Consult a doctor before starting if you have heart, lung, blood pressure, diabetes or joint conditions, or are pregnant. Stop immediately for chest pain, pain spreading to arm/jaw, fainting or severe breathlessness — call **112**. In heat, go early morning or evening and hydrate.

activity.prompt: Using 220 − age, what is the estimated maximum heart rate of a 50-year-old?

quiz.q: Using 220 − age, a 20-year-old's estimated max HR is…
quiz.why: The estimate of maximum heart rate is 220 − age. For a 20-year-old, 220 − 20 = 200 beats per minute.

quiz.q: Why might someone on beta-blockers use RPE instead of heart rate?
quiz.why: Beta-blockers can lower and blunt the heart rate, so heart rate may not show effort correctly. RPE (rating of perceived exertion) measures how hard it feels instead.

quiz.q: RPE 3–4 out of 10 is roughly…
quiz.why: On a 0–10 effort scale, 3–4 is moderate effort. You are breathing harder but can still talk. Vigorous is about 7–8 and maximal is 10.

quiz.q: Chest pain spreading to the arm during exercise means…
quiz.why: Chest pain that spreads to the arm can be a sign of a heart attack. Stop exercising and call 112 immediately; do not push through it.

quiz.q: A walk–run plan works mainly because…
quiz.why: A walk–run plan builds fitness gradually and consistently, so the body adapts without too much strain. It is not meant to be very intense.

lessons.title: HIIT: high-intensity interval training, safely

story.title: Twenty minutes in a hostel room

scenes.text: Aman, 20, an engineering student in a small hostel room in Kota, has no gym and little time.
He learns a bodyweight HIIT session: 30 seconds hard, 30 seconds easy.
At first he goes all-out with sloppy form and his knees ache.
He slows down, fixes his form, and does it 2–3 times a week. He feels fitter in a month.

steps.title: What HIIT is
steps.body:
**High-intensity interval training** alternates short bursts of hard effort (for example RPE 7–9) with easy recovery. Sessions are short (10–25 minutes plus warm-up) and can improve aerobic fitness efficiently.

Examples:
- **30:30** — 30 s hard, 30 s easy, × 8–10.
- **40:20** — 40 s hard, 20 s rest.
- **Tabata-style** — 20 s very hard, 10 s rest, × 8 (4 minutes); very demanding — not for beginners.

steps.title: A beginner bodyweight HIIT
steps.body:
Warm-up 5 minutes (march, arm circles, squats). Then 2 rounds of:

- 30 s **brisk marching or jogging on the spot** / 30 s rest
- 30 s **squats** / 30 s rest
- 30 s **incline push-ups** (hands on a bed or wall) / 30 s rest
- 30 s **step-ups** on a low, stable step / 30 s rest
- 30 s **mountain climbers (slow)** / 30 s rest

Cool down 5 minutes. Do 2–3 times a week, not on consecutive days.

steps.title: Who should be careful
steps.body:
Consult a doctor before HIIT if you have heart disease, high blood pressure, diabetes, are pregnant, are older and unaccustomed to exercise, or have joint problems. Beginners should first build a base of moderate activity for a few weeks.

**Form beats speed**: when form breaks down, slow down or stop. Low-impact options (marching instead of jumping, step-ups instead of jump squats) protect joints.

steps.title: Common HIIT mistakes
steps.body:
- Doing HIIT every day — you need recovery.
- Choosing complex jumping moves too soon.
- No warm-up.
- Thinking 'more sweat = better'. Quality matters more.

activity.prompt: Beginner HIIT session (about 20 minutes). Tick as you go.
items: 5-minute warm-up: march, arm circles, slow squats
Round 1: marching/jogging on the spot 30 s, rest 30 s
Round 1: squats 30 s, rest 30 s
Round 1: incline push-ups 30 s, rest 30 s
Round 1: step-ups 30 s, rest 30 s
Round 1: slow mountain climbers 30 s, rest 30 s
Round 2: repeat all five
5-minute cool-down and stretch
Note your RPE (0–10) for the hardest interval

quiz.q: HIIT alternates…
options: Short hard efforts and easy recovery
quiz.why: HIIT (high-intensity interval training) alternates short, hard efforts with easy recovery periods. Long slow running is a different type of training.

quiz.q: How often should a beginner do HIIT?
options: 2–3 times a week, not on consecutive days
quiz.why: A beginner should do HIIT 2–3 times a week, not on consecutive days. Hard sessions need recovery time between them.

quiz.q: When form breaks down during an interval you should…
quiz.why: When form breaks down, injury risk goes up, so slow down or stop. Going faster or holding your breath would make it worse.

quiz.q: A Tabata-style protocol is…
quiz.why: A Tabata protocol is 20 seconds of very hard work, then 10 seconds of rest, repeated 8 times. That totals 4 minutes and is very demanding.

questions.q: WHO: adults should do how many minutes of moderate activity per week (minimum)?
questions.why: WHO recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week for adults (up to 300 for extra benefit). 60 minutes is the daily figure for children.

questions.q: A warm-up should come…
questions.why: A warm-up comes before exercise. It raises body temperature and prepares your muscles and joints. After exercise comes the cool-down.

questions.q: Being able to talk but not sing indicates…
questions.why: Being able to talk but not sing is the sign of moderate intensity. At maximal effort, you can hardly speak.

questions.q: Children 5–17 should average at least…
questions.why: Children and teenagers aged 5–17 should average at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity a day.

questions.q: Long static stretches right before sprinting may…
questions.why: Long static stretches right before a sprint may slightly reduce power. Dynamic movements are a better warm-up.

questions.q: Estimated max HR for a 40-year-old?
questions.why: Estimated maximum heart rate = 220 − age = 220 − 40 = 180 beats per minute.

questions.q: The 'P' in RAMP stands for…
questions.why: In RAMP, the P stands for Potentiate: gradually building up to the speed and intensity of the main session.

questions.q: Older adults should add which on 3+ days a week?
questions.why: Older adults should add balance and strength activities on 3 or more days a week. Walking alone does not do this.

questions.q: Who should consult a doctor before HIIT?
options: People with heart disease or uncontrolled blood pressure
questions.why: People with heart disease or uncontrolled blood pressure should check with a doctor before HIIT, because very hard effort puts extra strain on the heart.

questions.q: For a 30-year-old, the moderate HR zone (64–76% of estimated max) is about…
questions.why: Max HR is 220 − 30 = 190. The moderate zone is 64–76%: 0.64 × 190 ≈ 122 and 0.76 × 190 ≈ 144 bpm.

questions.q: Why are heart rate formulas only estimates?
options: Individual max HR can vary by 10 or more beats
questions.why: Formulas like 220 − age are only estimates. A person's real maximum heart rate can differ by 10 or more beats from the formula.

questions.q: Someone does 100 min moderate + 30 min vigorous weekly. Do they meet the minimum adult aerobic guideline?
questions.why: Vigorous minutes count double, so 30 vigorous minutes ≈ 60 moderate minutes. 100 + 60 = 160, which is above the 150-minute minimum.

questions.q: Which sign during exercise is an emergency?
options: Chest pain spreading to the jaw or arm
questions.why: Chest pain spreading to the jaw or arm may mean a heart attack. Stop and call 112. Sweating alone is normal in exercise.
