courses.title: Football from zero: the Laws, offside and positions
courses.summary: The pitch, the ball, how a match flows, the offside Law made simple, fouls, cards and restarts, and what every position on the field actually does.
outcomes: Learners can describe the pitch markings and how a match starts, stops and restarts
Learners can decide whether a player is offside in common situations
Learners can tell direct from indirect free kicks and know when a penalty is given
Learners can explain the roles of goalkeeper, defenders, midfielders and forwards

lessons.title: The pitch, the match and restarts

scenes.text: Lalremruati, 10, from Aizawl in Mizoram — where football is everywhere — joins a girls' league team.
In her first match the ball goes out over the goal line and she runs to take a throw-in. Everyone laughs kindly.
Her coach, Mr. Lalrinsanga, draws the pitch on a whiteboard and explains every line and restart.
Next week she takes a perfect corner that leads to a goal.

steps.title: The pitch
steps.body:
- A rectangle with two long **touchlines** and two short **goal lines**.
- The **halfway line** divides it; the **centre circle** has a radius of 9.15 m (10 yards).
- Each end has a **goal**: 7.32 m wide and 2.44 m high (8 yards by 8 feet).
- The **goal area** (the small box) and the **penalty area** (the big box, 16.5 m / 18 yards out) are marked in front of each goal.
- The **penalty mark** is 11 m from the goal line.
- **Corner arcs** sit at each corner.

steps.title: How a match works
steps.body:
- Two teams of **11 players**, including one **goalkeeper** each. A match can't start or continue if a team has fewer than **7**.
- Two halves of **45 minutes**, with a half-time interval (up to 15 minutes). The referee adds time for stoppages.
- A **goal** is scored when the **whole ball crosses the goal line** between the posts and under the crossbar.
- The ball is **out of play** only when the **whole ball** has crossed a touchline or goal line (on the ground or in the air) or the referee stops play.
- Many competitions allow up to **five substitutes**.

steps.title: Restarts
steps.body:
- **Kick-off**: starts each half and restarts after a goal; the ball can be kicked in any direction.
- **Throw-in**: when the ball crosses the **touchline**. Taken with **both hands, from behind and over the head**, with **both feet on the ground** on or behind the line. A goal cannot be scored directly from a throw-in.
- **Goal kick**: when the attacking team last touched the ball over the **goal line** (not a goal).
- **Corner kick**: when the defending team last touched it over their own goal line.
- **Free kicks and penalty kicks** after fouls (lesson 3).
- **Dropped ball**: after the referee stops play for, say, an injury.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the ball is out when it's on the line — it's still **in** until the whole ball crosses.
- Lifting a foot during a throw-in → a foul throw, and the other team gets the throw.
- Confusing goal kicks and corners: who touched it last decides.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Watch 10 minutes of any match and call every restart out loud before the referee signals: 'Throw-in, blue!', 'Corner, red!'. Count how many you get right.

activity.prompt: Which restart is it?

items.text: Attacker shoots wide over the goal line
Defender heads the ball over their own goal line
Ball rolls over the touchline off a midfielder
Goalkeeper tips a shot over the crossbar
A long pass sails over the touchline
Striker's cross goes out over the far goal line untouched

quiz.q: When is a goal scored?
options: When the ball hits the post
When part of the ball crosses the line
When the whole ball crosses the goal line between posts and under the bar
quiz.why: A goal counts only when the whole ball has crossed the goal line, between the posts and under the crossbar. Part of the ball over the line is not enough.

quiz.q: How is a throw-in taken?
options: Both hands from behind and over the head, both feet on the ground
quiz.why: A throw-in is taken with both hands, from behind and over the head, with both feet on the ground. One-handed, kicked or bounced throws are not allowed.

quiz.q: A defender last touches the ball over their own goal line (no goal). The restart is…
quiz.why: If a defender is the last to touch the ball before it crosses their own goal line (and no goal is scored), the attacking team gets a corner kick. A goal kick would be if an attacker touched it last.

quiz.q: How far is the penalty mark from the goal line?
quiz.why: The penalty mark is 11 metres (12 yards) from the goal line. 9.15 m is the free-kick wall distance, and 16.5 m is the edge of the penalty area.

quiz.q: Can a goal be scored directly from a throw-in?
quiz.why: A goal cannot be scored directly from a throw-in. If the ball goes straight into the goal, it is a goal kick or corner, depending on which goal.

lessons.title: Offside, made simple

scenes.text: Carlos, 12, plays in São Paulo, Brazil. He keeps scoring — and the assistant referee keeps raising the flag.
'I'm not offside! I was behind the ball!' he argues. 'You were beyond the last defender when the pass was played,' says the referee.
His coach, Ana, sets up cones and has him time his runs to the moment the pass is struck.
Carlos learns to stay level and run late. His goals double — and the flags stop.

steps.title: Offside position
steps.body:
A player is in an **offside position** if:

- any part of their **head, body or feet** is in the **opponents' half** (not counting the halfway line), **and**
- that part is **nearer to the opponents' goal line than both the ball and the second-last opponent** (the goalkeeper usually counts as one of the last two).

Arms and hands are **not** counted (for goalkeepers too). **Level** with the second-last opponent, or level with the ball, is **onside**.

steps.title: Being in an offside position isn't an offence by itself
steps.body:
It only becomes an **offside offence** if, **at the moment a team-mate plays or touches the ball**, the player in an offside position becomes **involved in active play** by:

- **Interfering with play**: playing or touching the ball.
- **Interfering with an opponent**: e.g., blocking the keeper's line of sight or challenging for the ball.
- **Gaining an advantage**: playing a ball that rebounds off the post, the bar or an opponent, or a save.

The moment that matters is **when the pass is played**, not where the player is when they receive it.

steps.title: No offside from these
steps.body:
There is **no offside offence** if a player receives the ball directly from a **goal kick, throw-in or corner kick**. And you can **never** be offside in your **own half**.

The punishment for an offside offence is an **indirect free kick** to the defending team, from where the offence happened.

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body:
1. Striker is 1 m beyond the last defender (keeper behind them) when the winger crosses. She scores. → **Offside.**
2. Striker is level with the last defender when the pass is played, then runs past and scores. → **Onside.**
3. Striker is in an offside position but walks back and doesn't touch the ball or affect anyone; team-mate scores. → **Not an offence.**
4. Throw-in directly to a player behind the defence. → **No offside** from a throw-in.

steps.title: How attackers beat the offside trap
steps.body:
- **Curve your run** along the defensive line, then burst as the passer's foot goes back.
- **Watch the passer and the defenders** at the same time (scan).
- Start your run from **level or behind**, not from beyond the line.

statements.s: A player in their own half can be offside.
statements.why: You can never be offside in your own half.

statements.s: Being level with the second-last defender is onside.
statements.why: Level is onside.

statements.s: You can be offside directly from a corner kick.
statements.why: No offside from corners, throw-ins or goal kicks.

statements.s: Offside position is judged when the pass is played, not when it's received.
statements.why: The moment the team-mate plays or touches the ball is what counts.

statements.s: An offside offence is punished with a penalty kick.
statements.why: It's an indirect free kick.

statements.s: A player's arms count when judging offside position.
statements.why: Arms and hands are not considered.

quiz.q: Offside position is judged at the moment…
options: A team-mate plays or touches the ball
quiz.why: Offside position is judged at the moment a team-mate plays or touches the ball. Where the player is when they later receive it does not matter for position.

quiz.q: Which body part is NOT considered for offside position?
quiz.why: Arms and hands are not counted in offside position, because they are not scoring parts. The head, torso and feet are counted.

quiz.q: Restart after an offside offence?
quiz.why: After an offside offence, the other team takes an indirect free kick from where the offence happened. A direct kick or penalty is for fouls.

quiz.q: A player in an offside position doesn't touch the ball or affect any opponent. Offence?
quiz.why: Being in an offside position is not an offence in itself. It only counts if the player becomes involved in active play, for example by touching the ball or affecting an opponent.

quiz.q: From which restart can you NOT be offside?
options: A rebound off a defender's deliberate save
quiz.why: There is no offside offence from a throw-in, goal kick or corner kick. An attacker can wait in front of the defence for a throw-in without being offside.

sources: IFAB Laws of the Game, Law 11

lessons.title: Fouls, cards, free kicks and penalties

scenes.text: Imran, 15, from Kozhikode, Kerala, is frustrated after a missed chance and lunges in with studs up.
The referee shows a red card. His team plays 40 minutes with ten men and loses.
His coach explains the difference between careless, reckless and excessive force — and why tackling is a skill, not anger.
Imran apologises to the opponent. Next season he's the team's cleanest, smartest defender.

steps.title: Direct free kick offences
steps.body:
A **direct free kick** (you can score directly) is given if a player, in a way the referee considers **careless, reckless or using excessive force**: kicks, trips, pushes, jumps at, charges, strikes or tackles/challenges an opponent. Also: **holding** an opponent, **deliberate handball**, **biting or spitting** at someone, or throwing an object at the ball or a person.

- **Careless**: lack of attention → free kick only.
- **Reckless**: disregard for danger → **yellow card**.
- **Excessive force**: endangering safety → **red card**.

steps.title: Indirect free kick offences
steps.body:
An **indirect free kick** (the ball must touch another player before a goal can count — the referee raises an arm) is given for things like:

- **Playing in a dangerous manner** (e.g., a high kick near someone's head) without contact.
- **Impeding** an opponent without contact.
- **Offside**.
- The **goalkeeper** handling the ball from a **deliberate kick-pass by a team-mate** (the back-pass rule) or directly from a team-mate's throw-in.
- Preventing the keeper releasing the ball.

steps.title: Penalty kicks
steps.body: If a defending player commits a **direct free kick offence inside their own penalty area**, the attacking team gets a **penalty kick** from the penalty mark (11 m). Only the kicker and the defending goalkeeper are allowed inside the area and in front of the ball until it's kicked; the keeper must stay on the goal line between the posts, with at least part of one foot on or in line with the line at the kick.

steps.title: Yellow and red cards
steps.body:
**Yellow card (caution)** examples: reckless fouls, unsporting behaviour, dissent, delaying the restart, persistent fouling, not respecting the 9.15 m distance.

**Red card (sending off)** examples: serious foul play, violent conduct, biting/spitting, denying an obvious goal-scoring opportunity by a deliberate handball or (in many cases) by a foul, offensive or abusive language or gestures, and **a second yellow card** in the same match. A sent-off player can't be replaced.

steps.title: Free kick walls and advantage
steps.body:
- Defenders must be at least **9.15 m (10 yards)** from the ball at a free kick. When three or more defenders form a wall, attackers must stay at least 1 m away from it.
- The referee may play **advantage** — letting play continue if stopping would hurt the fouled team — and can still caution the offender later.

a.text: You're the referee. A defender slides in, misses the ball, and catches the attacker's ankle with no real force. It's outside the box. Decision?

choices.label: Direct free kick, no card (careless)
choices.feedback: Right — careless challenge, free kick only.

choices.label: Red card
choices.feedback: Too harsh — no excessive force here.

b.text: Later, a defender inside his own penalty area pulls an attacker's shirt and stops him reaching a cross. Decision?

choices.label: Penalty kick
choices.feedback: Holding is a direct free kick offence; inside the area → penalty.

choices.label: Indirect free kick
choices.feedback: Holding is a direct free kick offence.

c.text: Think again: was it careless, reckless or excessive force?

choices.label: Careless → direct free kick, no card
choices.feedback: That's it.

d.text: Holding is in the direct free kick list. Where did it happen?

choices.label: Inside the penalty area → penalty kick
choices.feedback: Correct.

end1.text: Great refereeing! You judged force correctly and applied the penalty rule.

quiz.q: A reckless tackle should be punished with…
options: A free kick and a yellow card
A free kick and a red card
quiz.why: A reckless tackle is punished with a free kick and a yellow card (caution). A red card is for serious foul play or excessive force.

quiz.q: A direct free kick offence by a defender in their own penalty area gives…
quiz.why: A direct free-kick offence by a defender inside their own penalty area is punished with a penalty kick.

quiz.q: How far must defenders be from a free kick?
quiz.why: Defenders must be at least 9.15 m (10 yards) from the ball at a free kick, until it is kicked. This stops them from blocking the kick.

quiz.q: A goalkeeper picks up a deliberate kick-pass from a team-mate. Restart?
quiz.why: A goalkeeper may not handle a deliberate kick-pass from a team-mate. The restart is an indirect free kick, from where the keeper handled it.

quiz.q: Two yellow cards in the same match lead to…
quiz.why: Two yellow cards (cautions) in the same match lead to a red card, so the player is sent off. A single yellow is only a caution.

sources: IFAB Laws of the Game, Law 12–14

lessons.title: Positions and roles: who does what

scenes.text: Aditi, 11, in Goa, always chases the ball everywhere — like everyone else in her team.
'We look like a swarm of bees,' laughs coach Fatima. She gives each girl a zone and a job.
Aditi becomes a central midfielder: she scans, passes and links defence to attack.
The team stops swarming, starts passing, and wins its first tournament.

steps.title: Goalkeeper
steps.body: The only player who may **handle the ball** — and only **inside their own penalty area**. Jobs: stop shots, catch crosses, organise the defence by talking, and start attacks with throws and kicks. Wears a different colour.

steps.title: Defenders
steps.body:
- **Centre-backs (CB)**: the central defensive pair (or three). Win headers, tackle, block shots, mark strikers, start build-up with calm passes.
- **Full-backs (RB/LB)**: defend the wide areas, stop wingers, and **overlap** to support attacks.
- **Wing-backs**: in systems with three centre-backs, they cover the whole flank — very fit players.

steps.title: Midfielders
steps.body:
- **Defensive midfielder (DM)**: shields the defence, breaks up attacks, keeps possession simple.
- **Central midfielder (CM)**: the engine — passes, supports both attack and defence, covers huge distances.
- **Attacking midfielder (AM / 'number 10')**: plays between the opponent's lines, creates chances.
- **Wide midfielders / wingers**: provide width, dribble, cross and cut inside to shoot.

steps.title: Forwards
steps.body:
- **Centre-forward / striker**: scores goals, holds the ball up, makes runs behind the defence, presses defenders.
- **Second striker or false 9**: drops deeper to link play and drag defenders out of position.

Modern football expects **everyone** to defend and attack to some degree.

steps.title: Try this: role-watch
steps.body: Pick one player in a televised match and watch only them for 10 minutes. Note: where they stand when their team has the ball, where they go when they lose it, how often they scan (look over their shoulder). You'll learn more than watching the ball.

activity.prompt: Match the position to its main job.
pairs: Can handle the ball in own penalty area; organises defence
Wins headers and marks the striker centrally
Defends wide and overlaps to attack
Shields the defence and breaks up attacks
Scores goals and runs behind the defence

quiz.q: Where may a goalkeeper handle the ball?
quiz.why: A goalkeeper can use their hands only inside their own penalty area. Outside it, the keeper is treated like any other player.

quiz.q: Which player most often 'overlaps' the winger?
quiz.why: Full-backs often overlap, running outside the winger to give width. This gives the attack an extra option.

quiz.q: A player who shields the defence and breaks up attacks is a…
quiz.why: A defensive midfielder shields the defence and breaks up opposition attacks. This is different from a winger or a striker.

quiz.q: Why did Aditi's coach give zones?
options: To stop the 'swarm' and create passing options
quiz.why: Children often swarm around the ball. Zones spread players out, so there is space and more passing options for team-mates.

questions.q: How many players per team, including the goalkeeper?
questions.why: Each team has eleven players on the pitch, including the goalkeeper.

questions.q: How long is each half in a standard match?
questions.why: A standard match has two halves of 45 minutes each, 90 minutes in total (plus stoppage time).

questions.q: Ball crosses the touchline. Restart?
questions.why: When the whole ball crosses the touchline (side line), play restarts with a throw-in for the other team. A goal kick or corner is for the goal line.

questions.q: Which player may handle the ball in the penalty area?
questions.why: Only the goalkeeper can handle the ball inside their own penalty area. Any other player doing so would commit a handball offence.

questions.q: Is level with the second-last opponent onside?
questions.why: A player level with the second-last opponent is onside. They need to be nearer the goal line than both the ball and the second-last opponent to be offside.

questions.q: Excessive force in a tackle results in…
questions.why: Using excessive force in a tackle is serious foul play and gets a red card. A yellow card is for lesser offences like reckless play.

questions.q: Fewest players a team needs to start or continue a match?
questions.why: A team must have at least seven players to start or continue a match. With fewer than seven the match cannot go on.

questions.q: Restart after a goalkeeper handles a deliberate back-pass kick?
questions.why: If a goalkeeper handles a ball deliberately kicked to them by a team-mate, the restart is an indirect free kick to the other team.

questions.q: Can you be offside from a goal kick?
questions.why: There is no offside offence when a player receives the ball directly from a goal kick.

questions.q: A striker in an offside position gains an advantage by scoring from a rebound off the post. Decision?
questions.why: A player in an offside position who gets the ball from a rebound off the post gains an advantage, so it is an offside offence. The goal would not count.

questions.q: When does a ball on the touchline count as out?
options: When most of it is over
Only when the whole ball has crossed
questions.why: The ball is out only when the whole ball has crossed the line. If any part still touches the line, it is still in play.

questions.q: Which describes the goalkeeper's position at a penalty kick?
options: On the goal line between the posts, at least part of one foot on or in line with it at the kick
questions.why: At a penalty kick, the goalkeeper must stay on the goal line between the posts, with at least part of one foot on or in line with it when the ball is kicked. Standing on the mark or moving forward is not allowed.

questions.q: A defender impedes an attacker without contact. Restart?
questions.why: Impeding an opponent without contact is an indirect free kick offence, and it is that even inside the area. A penalty is for a direct free-kick offence such as a trip or push.

courses.title: Ball skills: first touch, passing, dribbling, shooting and heading safely
courses.summary: Master the core technical skills with clear coaching points, common errors and drills you can do alone with a wall or with friends.
outcomes: Learners can control the ball with different surfaces and scan before receiving
Learners can play accurate short and long passes
Learners can dribble with close control, change pace and direction, and use simple feints
Learners can strike the ball with the laces and side-foot for placement
Learners can explain heading safety and concussion rules

lessons.title: First touch and passing

scenes.text: Ravi, 12, lives in a crowded lane in Kolkata with no football ground nearby.
Every evening he passes a ball against the wall of the old warehouse: right foot, left foot, 500 passes.
At the club trials, the coach notices his first touch never lets the ball bounce away.
'Where did you train?' 'With a wall, sir.' Ravi gets selected.

steps.title: Scan before you receive
steps.body: Before the ball arrives, **look over your shoulder** to see where team-mates, opponents and space are. Top midfielders scan many times in the seconds before receiving. Scanning tells your first touch **where to go**.

steps.title: First touch
steps.body:
- Get your body **in line** with the ball, on your toes.
- Choose the surface: **inside of the foot** (most control), **outside**, **sole**, **thigh**, **chest**.
- **Cushion** the ball by relaxing the surface and drawing it back slightly as the ball arrives.
- Better: take a **directional first touch** — move the ball into space, away from pressure, ready for your next action.
- Use your **back foot** (the foot further from where the ball comes from) to open your body to the field.

steps.title: The side-foot (inside) pass
steps.body:
- **Plant foot** beside the ball, pointing at your target, about a ball's width away.
- Turn the passing foot out so the **inside of the foot** faces the target; **lock the ankle** (toes up).
- Strike the **middle of the ball** — not under it — and follow through towards the target.
- Head steady, eyes on the ball at contact.

For **longer passes**, approach at a slight angle, strike with the **instep/laces** area, lean back slightly to lift it, or keep over the ball to drive it low.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- **Floppy ankle** → weak, wobbly passes.
- **Plant foot too far behind** → the ball pops up.
- **Looking only at the ball** → no idea where to pass next. Scan first!
- Always passing with the strong foot — train the **weaker foot** every day.

steps.title: Wall drill
steps.body: Stand 5 m from a wall. Pass with the right foot, control with the left, pass with the left, control with the right. Count passes in 60 seconds. Then step back to 10 m. Record your best score each week.

activity.prompt: Solo passing & first-touch programme (15 minutes)
items: Warm-up: 3 min jog and dynamic stretches
50 wall passes, right foot, ankle locked
50 wall passes, left foot
20 directional first touches: receive and move the ball to the side into space
20 passes on the move: touch, step, pass
Scan over your shoulder before every 5th pass
Cool-down: calf and hamstring stretch

quiz.q: Why scan before receiving?
options: To know where space and team-mates are before the ball arrives
quiz.why: Scanning means looking around before the ball arrives, so you know where space and team-mates are. This helps you take a better first touch.

quiz.q: For a side-foot pass, the ankle should be…
quiz.why: For a side-foot pass, the ankle should be locked, with the toes up. A floppy ankle makes the pass weak and inaccurate.

quiz.q: Where should the plant foot point?
quiz.why: The plant foot should point at the target. The ball tends to go in the direction the plant foot points.

quiz.q: A directional first touch…
options: Moves the ball into space ready for the next action
quiz.why: A directional first touch moves the ball into space in the direction you want to go next. This saves time and helps you escape pressure.

lessons.title: Dribbling and 1v1 moves

scenes.text: Amara, 13, plays street football in Lagos, Nigeria, where the ball is always close to her feet.
She practises one move — the step-over — 1,000 times until she can do it without looking.
In a match, she drops her shoulder, steps over, and accelerates past the full-back.
Her cross is headed in. 'One move, mastered, is worth ten you half-know,' says her coach.

steps.title: Close control
steps.body:
- Keep the ball **close** — within a stride — when opponents are near.
- Use **many small touches** with the inside, outside and sole of both feet.
- Stay **low and balanced**, knees bent, arms out slightly for balance.
- **Head up** between touches to see space and defenders.

steps.title: Change of pace and direction
steps.body:
The most effective dribble is often simple: **slow down, then explode**. Defenders hate sudden acceleration.

- **Speed dribble**: in open space, push the ball further ahead with the laces/outside of the foot and sprint.
- **Cut**: drag or chop the ball sharply with the inside or outside of the foot to change direction.

steps.title: Three moves to master
steps.body:
- **Body feint / shoulder drop**: dip one shoulder as if going that way, then go the other.
- **Step-over**: circle your foot around the front of the ball (inside to outside) without touching it, then take it away with the other foot's outside.
- **Cruyff turn**: shape to pass or cross, then drag the ball behind your standing leg with the inside of the foot and turn away.

Practise slowly, then at match speed, then against a passive defender, then a real one.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dribbling with the **head down** → running into defenders or missing a free team-mate.
- Doing tricks **too far from** the defender (they have time to react) or **too close** (they can tackle).
- Dribbling in your own defensive third when a simple pass is safer.

steps.title: Cone slalom
steps.body: Set 6 cones (or slippers) 1 m apart. Dribble through using: right foot only, left foot only, inside-outside, sole rolls. Time each run and try to beat it while keeping every cone standing.

activity.prompt: Put the Cruyff turn in order.
items: Approach the ball as if to pass or cross
Plant your standing foot beside and slightly ahead of the ball
Instead of kicking, place the inside of the kicking foot on the far side of the ball
Drag the ball behind your standing leg
Turn your body 180° and accelerate away

quiz.q: What's often the most effective dribble?
options: Slow down, then explode with a change of pace
quiz.why: A change of pace is often the most effective dribble: slow down to draw the defender in, then accelerate past. Tricks every time or running straight are easy to defend.

quiz.q: In a step-over, your foot…
options: Circles round the ball without touching it
quiz.why: In a step-over, the foot circles around the ball without touching it. It is a fake to make the defender move the wrong way.

quiz.q: Why keep your head up when dribbling?
options: To see space, defenders and team-mates
quiz.why: Keeping your head up while dribbling lets you see space, defenders and team-mates. Then you can choose between dribbling, passing and shooting.

quiz.q: Where is risky dribbling least wise?
quiz.why: Risky dribbling is least wise in your own defensive third, because losing the ball near your own goal gives the opponents a chance to score.

lessons.title: Shooting and finishing

scenes.text: Meera, 14, from Bhubaneswar, blasts every shot as hard as she can. Most fly over.
Her coach hangs two old bibs in the bottom corners of the goal: 'Hit the bibs, not the net.'
She learns to side-foot finishes close in and to keep her knee over the ball for driven shots.
Her goals tripled in a season — mostly low into the corners.

steps.title: Placement before power
steps.body: Most goals at every level are scored by **accurate** shots, often low and into the corners, rather than the hardest ones. A low shot is hard for a keeper to reach quickly and can deflect or be spilled.

steps.title: The driven (laces) shot
steps.body:
- Approach at a **slight angle**.
- **Plant foot beside the ball**, pointing at the target.
- **Knee and head over the ball**, toes pointed down, ankle locked.
- Strike through the **middle of the ball** with the **laces**.
- Land on your shooting foot — follow through towards the target.

Leaning back = ball goes high. Over the ball = low and hard.

steps.title: Side-foot finish and other finishes
steps.body:
- **Side-foot finish**: inside of the foot for accuracy when close to goal — like a firm pass into the corner.
- **Volley**: watch the ball onto your foot, keep over it, short swing.
- **Chip**: when the keeper rushes out, get under the ball with a short stab.
- **Composure**: pick your spot early; look at the keeper's position, then the ball at contact.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- **Leaning back** → over the bar.
- **Toe-poking** with no control (useful only in emergencies).
- **Changing your mind** at the last moment.
- **Looking up at contact** → mishit. Look at the ball when you strike.

steps.title: Corner targets
steps.body: Place two targets (bags, bottles) in the bottom corners of a goal. From 12 m, take 10 shots with each foot: 3 points for a target hit, 1 for on target. Record and beat your score.

activity.prompt: Complete the coaching points for a driven shot.
activity.text: Plant your foot ___ the ball, keep your knee and head ___ the ball, and strike with your ___ with the ankle locked.

quiz.q: What usually matters more for scoring?
quiz.why: For scoring, placement is usually more important than power. A well-placed shot is hard for the keeper to reach, even if it is not very hard.

quiz.q: Why do shots fly over the bar?
quiz.why: Leaning back at contact lifts the ball up, so the shot flies over the bar. Keeping the knee over the ball keeps it low.

quiz.q: When is a chip useful?
quiz.why: A chip is useful when the goalkeeper rushes out, because it lifts the ball over them and into the goal.

quiz.q: For a close-range finish, which surface gives best accuracy?
quiz.why: At close range, the inside of the foot (side-foot) is the most accurate surface. Toe or heel kicks are hard to control.

lessons.title: Heading safely, concussion and staying injury-free

scenes.text: Tom, 15, in Glasgow, Scotland, clashes heads with an opponent going for a header.
He says he's fine, but he's dizzy and asks the same question twice.
His coach, Mrs. Singh, takes him off immediately — 'If in doubt, sit them out' — and he's checked by a doctor.
He follows a gradual return-to-play plan and is back two weeks later, symptom-free.

steps.title: Heading technique (for older players)
steps.body:
When heading is appropriate for your age:

- **Eyes open**, watching the ball; **mouth closed**.
- Contact with the **forehead** (the flat, hard part at the hairline), not the top of the head.
- **Neck firm**; power comes from bending the **upper body/back** and moving through the ball.
- Arms out for balance and protection — but **no elbows** into opponents.

steps.title: Limits on heading for children
steps.body: Because of concerns about repeated head impacts, several football associations — for example in **England and Scotland** — have issued guidance that limits or removes **heading practice for children**, and reduces repetitive heading in training for older players. Coaches should follow their own association's current guidance. Light balls and low numbers of repetitions are common recommendations when heading is taught.

steps.title: Concussion: if in doubt, sit them out
steps.body:
Signs after a knock to the head or body: **headache, dizziness, confusion, memory problems, nausea or vomiting, blurred vision, unusual behaviour, loss of consciousness**.

- **Remove the player** from play immediately — never return the same day.
- **Seek medical assessment**. Call **112** for loss of consciousness, worsening headache, repeated vomiting, seizures, weakness or neck pain.
- **Return gradually** under medical advice, following a step-by-step return-to-play plan.

steps.title: Preventing other common injuries
steps.body:
- Use a structured warm-up — programmes like **FIFA 11+** (running, strength, balance and jumping exercises) have been shown to reduce injuries in amateur players.
- **Shin guards** are compulsory in matches.
- Build **hamstring strength** (e.g., Nordic curls under supervision) and **ankle balance** (single-leg standing).
- Increase training load gradually; rest when you're sore or ill.

This is general education, not medical advice — see a doctor or physiotherapist for pain that persists.

a.text: In your U-16 match, a team-mate clashes heads and says, 'I'm OK, let me play.' He looks dazed. What do you do?

choices.label: Let him continue — he says he's fine
choices.feedback: Concussed players often say they're fine.

choices.label: Tell the coach and get him off the pitch
choices.feedback: Exactly — if in doubt, sit them out.

b.text: Five minutes later he's confused and feels sick. Now?

choices.label: Get him off immediately and get medical help; call 112 if symptoms worsen
choices.feedback: Right, but sooner is safer.

c.text: Off the pitch, he still has a headache. When can he play again?

choices.label: Not today; only after medical assessment and a gradual return plan
choices.feedback: Correct.

choices.label: Second half, if the headache eases
choices.feedback: Never return the same day after suspected concussion.

end1.text: You protected your friend's brain. That's real teamwork.

end2.text: He's getting help now. Next time, remove anyone with suspected concussion straight away.

quiz.q: Which part of the head should contact the ball?
quiz.why: The forehead is the flat, strong part of the head. It lets you see the ball and direct it, so it should be the contact area when heading.

quiz.q: After a suspected concussion, a player should…
options: Not return the same day and get medical assessment
Play on if they can walk
Have a sugary drink and continue
quiz.why: After a suspected concussion, the player must be removed from play and not return the same day. They need a medical assessment and a gradual return.

quiz.q: FIFA 11+ is…
quiz.why: FIFA 11+ is a structured warm-up programme designed to reduce injuries. It includes running, strength, balance and jumping exercises.

quiz.q: Why have some associations limited heading for children?
quiz.why: Some associations limit heading for children because of concern about the effects of repeated head impacts. It is a precaution.

quiz.q: Which sign means call 112?
options: Repeated vomiting or loss of consciousness
quiz.why: Repeated vomiting or loss of consciousness after a head injury are red flags needing urgent care, so call 112. Tiredness, thirst or muddy kit are not emergencies.

questions.q: Which surface gives most control for a short pass?
questions.why: The inside of the foot gives the most control for a short pass, because it is a broad, flat surface. The toe or heel gives little accuracy.

questions.q: Shin guards in matches are…
questions.why: Shin guards are compulsory equipment in matches, to protect the lower legs. A player without them may not take part.

questions.q: What should you do just before receiving a pass?
questions.why: Scan, meaning look around, just before receiving a pass. It shows you where team-mates and space are.

questions.q: For a driven shot, the knee should be…
questions.why: For a driven shot, the knee should be over the ball. This keeps the shot low. Leaning back would lift it over the bar.

questions.q: Which move drags the ball behind the standing leg?
questions.why: In the Cruyff turn, you drag the ball behind your standing leg and turn the other way. A step-over is a fake without touching the ball.

questions.q: A floppy ankle on a pass causes…
questions.why: A floppy ankle gives a weak, inaccurate pass. Locking the ankle gives a firm, accurate one.

questions.q: Which is the best response to a suspected concussion?
options: Remove from play and get medical assessment
questions.why: With a suspected concussion, remove the player from play and get a medical assessment. The rule is 'if in doubt, sit them out'.

questions.q: Most goals come from…
questions.why: Most goals come from accurate, often low shots, because they are hard for the keeper to reach. The hardest possible shots often miss the target.

questions.q: A directional first touch is used to…
options: Stop the ball completely every time
Move the ball away from pressure into space
questions.why: A directional first touch moves the ball away from pressure into space. This sets up the next action rather than stopping it dead.

questions.q: When performing a feint, the best distance from the defender is…
options: Close enough to commit them but not within tackling reach
questions.why: For a feint, be close enough to make the defender commit, but outside tackling reach. If too far away, they have time; too close, they can tackle.

questions.q: Which is part of the FIFA 11+ type warm-up?
questions.why: A FIFA 11+ type warm-up includes running, strength, balance and jumping (plyometric) exercises. It is more than just static stretching.

questions.q: A player feels fine 20 minutes after a head knock but had brief confusion. Return same day?
questions.why: Brief confusion after a head knock suggests concussion, even if the player feels fine later. Any suspected concussion means no return to play that day.

questions.q: Why is training the weaker foot important?
options: It doubles your options and makes you less predictable
questions.why: Training the weaker foot gives you more options and makes you less predictable. Defenders cannot just force you onto your weaker side.

courses.title: Tactics, formations, goalkeeping and the football pathway in India
courses.summary: Read the game like a coach: formations, principles of attack and defence, pressing and set pieces, the complete basics of goalkeeping, and how football is organised in India.
outcomes: Learners can describe 4-4-2, 4-3-3 and 3-5-2 and their strengths
Learners can explain width, depth, support, penetration, compactness and pressing
Learners can perform the goalkeeper's set position, catches, basic diving and distribution
Learners can describe the general pathway in Indian football

scenes.text: Daniel, a youth coach in Bengaluru, sees his team overrun in midfield every week in a 4-4-2.
He switches to 4-3-3: three central midfielders instead of two.
Now his team keeps the ball and the wingers stretch the opposition.
'Formations are just starting positions,' he tells the players. 'Principles win games.'

steps.title: Reading the numbers
steps.body: A formation lists outfield players from **defence to attack** (the goalkeeper isn't counted). **4-4-2** = 4 defenders, 4 midfielders, 2 forwards. Sometimes a middle line is split: **4-2-3-1** = 4 defenders, 2 defensive midfielders, 3 attacking midfielders, 1 striker.

Two banks of four plus two strikers.
- **Strengths**: simple, balanced, good width, two strikers to press and combine, compact defensive blocks.
- **Weaknesses**: can be outnumbered in central midfield by three-man midfields; gaps between the lines if not disciplined.

Four defenders, three central midfielders (often one holding), two wingers and a centre-forward.
- **Strengths**: control of central midfield, width from wingers, natural high pressing triangles.
- **Weaknesses**: full-backs can be exposed if wingers don't track back; the lone striker can be isolated.

steps.title: 3-5-2 (or 5-3-2 when defending)
steps.body:
Three centre-backs, two wing-backs, three central midfielders, two strikers.
- **Strengths**: extra centre-back for cover, numbers in midfield, two strikers.
- **Weaknesses**: wing-backs must cover the whole flank; space behind them can be attacked.

When defending, wing-backs drop and it becomes a **5-3-2**.

steps.title: Formations change during the game
steps.body: Teams look different **in possession** (e.g., a 4-3-3 becoming 3-2-5 when full-backs push on) and **out of possession** (dropping into a 4-5-1). Watch a team both when it has the ball and when it doesn't.

cards.back: Two banks of four, two strikers; simple and balanced, can be outnumbered centrally.
Three central midfielders, two wingers, one striker; controls midfield and presses well.
Three centre-backs, wing-backs, two strikers; becomes 5-3-2 when defending.
Two holding midfielders behind three attacking midfielders and one striker.
Not counted — numbers list outfield players from defence to attack.

quiz.q: In '4-3-3', the first number refers to…
quiz.why: In a formation such as 4-3-3, the numbers are listed from defence to attack. So the first number, 4, is the defenders (the goalkeeper is not counted).

quiz.q: A common weakness of 4-4-2 is…
options: Being outnumbered in central midfield by a three
quiz.why: A 4-4-2 has only two central midfielders. Against a three in midfield, it can be outnumbered and lose control of the middle.

quiz.q: In a 3-5-2, who covers the full flank?
quiz.why: In a 3-5-2, the wing-backs cover the whole flank, defending and attacking along the sideline, since there are only three centre-backs.

quiz.q: What does 'formations are starting positions' mean?
options: Shapes change in and out of possession
quiz.why: A formation shows the starting shape. In play, the shape changes in and out of possession as players move.

lessons.title: Principles of attack and defence, pressing and set pieces

scenes.text: An under-17 team in Shillong is 2–0 down at half-time, always passing sideways.
Coach Wanshan tells them: 'Width, depth, support — and someone must run behind!'
The full-backs push wide, the striker runs in behind, and midfielders offer angles.
They win 3–2. The principles worked better than any shouting.

steps.title: Principles of attack
steps.body:
- **Width**: players spread wide to stretch defenders.
- **Depth**: players ahead of and behind the ball so there are forward and backward options.
- **Support**: angles for the ball-carrier — triangles and diamonds.
- **Penetration**: passes, dribbles or runs that break lines and go behind the defence.
- **Mobility**: movement off the ball to drag defenders.
- **Improvisation/creativity** in the final third.

steps.title: Principles of defence
steps.body:
- **Delay**: the nearest defender (the 'first defender') slows the attacker, staying goal-side.
- **Cover**: a second defender supports at an angle behind.
- **Balance**: others cover dangerous space and runners.
- **Compactness**: stay close together between and across the lines so there's little space to play through.
- **Patience and discipline**: don't dive in.

steps.title: Pressing and transitions
steps.body:
- **Pressing** means hunting the ball as a group to win it back quickly, using **triggers** (a poor touch, a backward pass, a pass to a full-back near the touchline).
- **Transitions** are the seconds after the ball changes hands. Teams that react fastest — counter-attacking or immediately counter-pressing — gain a big advantage.
- A **high press** needs fitness and coordination; one player pressing alone just gets bypassed.

steps.title: Set pieces
steps.body:
A large share of goals come from **corners, free kicks and throw-ins**.

- Attacking: planned runs, blockers (without fouling), near-post flick-ons, a target zone for the delivery.
- Defending: **zonal** (defend areas), **man-marking**, or a mix; keep someone ready for the counter-attack.
- Practise them every week — it's 'free' improvement.

steps.title: Try this: tactical notebook
steps.body: Watch a half of any match. Every 5 minutes write: Is the team wide or narrow? Who presses first? How many players are behind the ball when they lose it? You'll start seeing the game like a coach.

activity.prompt: Attacking or defending principle?

quiz.q: What does 'width' in attack do?
options: Stretches the defence to create gaps
quiz.why: Width in attack stretches the defence sideways. This opens gaps between defenders for passes and runs.

quiz.q: The first defender's main job is to…
options: Delay the attacker and stay goal-side
quiz.why: The first defender should delay the attacker and stay goal-side. Diving in risks being beaten, while delay gives team-mates time to recover.

quiz.q: A 'pressing trigger' could be…
options: A poor touch by the opponent
A goal kick to your team
quiz.why: A pressing trigger is a cue for the team to press together, such as a poor touch by the opponent. It shows when the ball can be won.

quiz.q: Which statement about set pieces is true?
options: A large share of goals come from them
quiz.why: A large share of goals come from set pieces such as corners and free kicks. They can be practised, so teams train them.

lessons.title: Goalkeeping basics

scenes.text: Sana, 13, in Srinagar, is put in goal because she's tall. She's scared of the ball.
Her coach starts with soft balls and teaches the 'W' catch and how to fall safely.
He also teaches her to shout — 'Away!', 'Keeper's!', 'Man on!'
By spring, she's organising the whole defence and saved two penalties in a shoot-out.

steps.title: The set position
steps.body:
As a shot is about to be taken:

- Feet about shoulder-width, **weight on the balls of the feet**, knees bent.
- Body slightly forward, hands out in front at about waist height, palms facing the ball.
- Head still, eyes on the ball.
- Make a small **'set'** (stop moving) just before the shooter strikes, so you can push off in any direction.

**Positioning**: stand on the imaginary line from the ball to the **centre of the goal** to cover both posts best.

steps.title: Catching
steps.body:
- **Chest-to-head height**: the **'W' (contour) catch** — thumbs and index fingers nearly touching behind the ball, fingers spread.
- **Chest height**: scoop the ball into the chest, elbows close together.
- **Low balls**: get your body behind it; for a rolling ball, go down on one knee or bend with legs together, scoop it up.
- **Always get something behind the ball** — hands, body, legs.
- Secure it: bring the ball into the chest.

steps.title: Diving and getting up
steps.body:
- Step **towards** the ball (a short power step), then push off the near-side foot.
- Land on your **side**, not your elbow or stomach.
- Hands lead, the bottom hand behind the ball, top hand on top.
- If you can't hold it, **parry** it wide of the goal, not back into the middle.
- Learn on soft ground or mats, starting from kneeling.

steps.title: Distribution and communication
steps.body:
- **Throws**: rolling (bowling) for short, overarm for longer.
- **Kicks**: goal kicks and side-volleys/half-volleys from hands; short passes to defenders to build play.
- Keepers may handle the ball **only in their own penalty area**, and cannot handle a deliberate kick-pass or a direct throw-in from a team-mate.
- Recent Law changes have also tightened **how long a keeper may hold the ball** — check the current IFAB Laws for your competition.
- **Talk**: clear, early, short calls — 'Keeper's!', 'Away!', 'Time!', 'Man on!'

steps.title: Safety and common mistakes
steps.body:
- Use **proper gloves** and, for young keepers, padded clothing on hard grounds.
- **Fingers pointing at the ball** → finger injuries. Hands open, slightly angled.
- Diving **backwards** or landing on the stomach → winded, missed saves.
- Coming off the line late and hesitantly — **commit** or stay.

activity.prompt: Goalkeeper home and training routine
items: Warm-up: jog, skips, hip and shoulder mobility
20 'W' catches from a partner's throws at head height
20 chest catches, elbows close together
10 low scoops each side
Kneeling dives onto a soft surface: 5 each side
Footwork: shuffle across goal and set, 10 times
Practise 5 loud calls: 'Keeper's!', 'Away!', 'Time!', 'Man on!', 'Squeeze!'

quiz.q: The 'W' catch is used for balls at…
quiz.why: The W catch is used for balls from chest to head height. The thumbs and fingers form a W shape behind the ball.

quiz.q: Where should a keeper stand to cover both posts best?
options: Next to the near post always
On the line from the ball to the centre of the goal
quiz.why: The keeper should stand on the line from the ball to the centre of the goal. This covers both posts best by splitting the shooting angle.

quiz.q: If you can't catch a shot, you should…
options: Parry it wide of the goal
quiz.why: If a keeper cannot hold the shot, they should parry it wide of the goal. A rebound into the middle gives attackers an easy chance.

quiz.q: Why make a small 'set' before the shot?
options: To be balanced and ready to push off any direction
quiz.why: A small set before the shot makes the keeper balanced and ready to push off in any direction. Moving at the moment of the shot leaves them off-balance.

lessons.title: The football pathway in India

story.title: From Manipur to the national camp

scenes.text: Tomba, 12, from Imphal, plays barefoot in local tournaments every weekend.
His school enters the Subroto Cup, a famous inter-school tournament, and a scout notices him.
He joins a recognised academy, keeps studying, and plays in age-group leagues.
At 16 he's called to an age-group national camp. 'Patience and proper registration,' his coach reminds him.

steps.title: The general structure
steps.body:
- **AIFF** (All India Football Federation) is the national governing body, affiliated to FIFA.
- **State associations** organise state leagues and pick state teams (for example for the **Santosh Trophy**, the national championship for state teams).
- **District associations** run local leagues.
- **Clubs and academies** run youth teams in age-group leagues.
- Professional and semi-professional leagues include the **Indian Super League (ISL)** and the **I-League**; women play in the **Indian Women's League (IWL)**.

Structures and competition names can change; check your state association for current details.

steps.title: School football
steps.body:
- The **Subroto Cup** is a long-running national inter-school football tournament.
- School games through the **School Games Federation of India (SGFI)** include football.
- Many famous players were spotted in school or local tournaments — play as many recognised matches as possible.

steps.title: Practical steps
steps.body:
- Join a **registered club or academy** and get properly registered through the official system.
- Keep **age documents** ready; age fraud can lead to bans.
- Look for **grassroots festivals and trials** announced by official bodies.
- Keep up your studies; football also needs coaches (AIFF/AFC coaching licences), physios, analysts, referees and administrators.

steps.title: Red flags
steps.body:
- Agents demanding money for guaranteed trials abroad.
- Requests to change documents.
- Pressure to leave school or home without proper contracts and parental involvement.

Genuine opportunities come through registered clubs and official trials. Talk to parents and coaches; verify everything.

a.text: An 'agent' offers a trial in Europe for ₹3 lakh, payable this week, no written contract. What do you do?

choices.label: Pay before the offer goes
choices.feedback: Pressure and no paperwork are red flags.

choices.label: Tell parents and coach, ask for documents, verify with official bodies
choices.feedback: Very wise.

choices.label: Tell parents, keep evidence, report to cybercrime helpline 1930 or police
choices.feedback: Reporting helps protect others too.

c.text: The agent refuses to give documents. What's next?

choices.label: Walk away and keep playing in recognised leagues
choices.feedback: Right — real offers can be verified.

end1.text: You avoided a scam and stayed on the genuine path.

end2.text: A hard lesson. Genuine trials don't demand big upfront payments without paperwork.

quiz.q: India's national football governing body is…
quiz.why: India's national football governing body is the All India Football Federation (AIFF). The BCCI is cricket and NADA deals with anti-doping.

quiz.q: The Santosh Trophy is a championship for…
quiz.why: The Santosh Trophy is India's national football championship for state teams, not clubs or schools.

quiz.q: The Subroto Cup is a famous…
quiz.why: The Subroto Cup is a well-known national inter-school football tournament in India.

quiz.q: Which is a red flag?
options: An agent demanding money without a contract
A coach asking for age proof
quiz.why: An agent demanding money without a contract is a red flag. Paying for unverified trials is risky, while registered club trials and age checks are normal.

questions.q: In formation numbers, which player is not counted?
questions.why: Formation numbers count outfield players only. The goalkeeper is not counted, so 4-4-2 adds up to 10.

questions.q: Which formation has three centre-backs?
questions.why: 3-5-2 has three centre-backs in defence. In 4-3-3 and 4-4-2 there are four defenders.

questions.q: India's football federation is the…
questions.why: The All India Football Federation (AIFF) runs football in India. The BCCI governs cricket.

questions.q: Which is a principle of defence?
questions.why: Compactness, keeping the team close together, is a principle of defence. Width is a principle of attack.

questions.q: For a high shot, a keeper uses the…
questions.why: For a high shot, the keeper uses the W catch (contour catch), with the hands forming a W behind the ball. The long barrier is for low balls along the ground.

questions.q: Which formation gives three central midfielders?
questions.why: 4-3-3 has three central midfielders. 4-4-2 has two central midfielders and two wide ones.

questions.q: What is a transition in football?
questions.why: A transition is the moment after possession changes, from defence to attack or attack to defence. It is a key moment for quick reactions.

questions.q: A keeper can't hold a shot. Best option?
questions.why: If a keeper cannot hold a shot, they should parry it wide, away from danger. A parry to the centre gives attackers an easy rebound.

questions.q: Who should press in a high press?
options: The team in a coordinated way
questions.why: A high press works only when the whole team moves together, closing passing lanes and squeezing space. One striker alone is easily bypassed.

questions.q: A 3-5-2 is most vulnerable…
questions.why: A 3-5-2 uses wing-backs who push high up the pitch. This leaves space behind them, which the opponent can use, as only three centre-backs cover the width.

questions.q: A 4-3-3 often looks like what in possession when full-backs push on?
questions.why: When the full-backs push on and a midfielder drops in, a 4-3-3 can look like a 3-2-5 in possession. A 6-3-1 would be a defensive shape.

questions.q: The 'second defender' in defending principles provides…
options: Cover at an angle behind the first defender
questions.why: The second defender gives cover at an angle behind the first defender. If the first defender is beaten, the second is ready to step in.

questions.q: Where is a keeper's ideal position relative to the shooter?
options: Always on the goal line in the centre
On the line bisecting the angle between ball and the two posts
questions.why: The ideal position is on the line that splits the angle between the ball and the two posts. This covers both sides, not just the centre.

Learners can hold forehand and backhand grips and switch between them

lessons.title: The court, scoring and serving rules

scenes.text: Aisha, 12, from Hyderabad, plays badminton every evening in her colony — with no lines and her own rules.
At her first district tournament, the umpire calls 'Service fault!' twice. She doesn't know why.
Her coach shows her the service height rule and which court to serve from.
She wins her next match 21–17, 21–15 — with zero service faults.

steps.title: The court
steps.body:
- Court length **13.4 m**; width **6.1 m** for doubles and **5.18 m** for singles.
- The net is **1.524 m (5 ft) high at the centre** and 1.55 m at the posts.
- **Singles**: long and narrow — use the inner side lines and the back boundary line.
- **Doubles**: wide — outer side lines; for the **serve**, the **doubles long service line** (0.76 m inside the back line) is the back limit, so the doubles service box is wide but short.

steps.title: Rally-point scoring
steps.body:
- Every rally wins a point, whoever served.
- A game is won by the first to **21 points**, but you must lead by **2**. At **29–29**, the next point wins (so 30 is the maximum).
- A match is **best of three games**.
- There is a short interval when the leading side reaches **11**, and a break between games.
- The side that wins a rally serves next.

steps.title: Service rules
steps.body:
- Server and receiver stand in **diagonally opposite service courts**, feet in contact with the floor and **not touching the lines**, until the serve is made.
- In singles, serve from the **right** service court when your score is **even** (0, 2, 4…) and from the **left** when it's **odd**.
- The whole shuttle must be **below 1.15 m from the court surface** when hit (current BWF rule), and you hit the **base (cork) of the shuttle first**.
- One continuous forward swing — no feints or delays once the serve starts.
- The serve must land in the receiver's diagonal service court; landing on the line is **in**.

steps.title: Common faults
steps.body:
- Serving with the shuttle **too high**.
- Stepping on a line or moving the feet before the serve.
- A **double hit** or carrying the shuttle (slinging it).
- Touching the net with the racket or body during play.
- Shuttle hitting your body — it's your fault.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Play a practice game with a friend where you **say the score aloud before every serve**, server's score first. Check you're serving from the right court for even, left for odd.

statements.s: A badminton game is won at 21 points by a 2-point lead, with 30 as the maximum.
statements.why: At 29–29, the next point wins.

statements.s: In singles, you serve from the left court when your score is even.
statements.why: Even score = right court; odd = left.

statements.s: A shuttle landing on the line is in.
statements.why: Lines are part of the court.

statements.s: You can only score a point when you are serving.
statements.why: Rally-point scoring: every rally wins a point.

statements.s: Touching the net with your racket during a rally is a fault.
statements.why: Touching the net is a fault.

quiz.q: How many points normally win a badminton game?
quiz.why: A badminton game is played to 21 points, but you must win by 2. The 11-point and 15-point formats are older ones.

quiz.q: Score 29–29. What happens?
quiz.why: If the score reaches 29–29, the next point wins the game, so 30 is the maximum score. Before that you need a 2-point lead.

quiz.q: In singles, with your score at 7, you serve from…
quiz.why: In singles you serve from the right court when your score is even and from the left court when it is odd. 7 is odd, so you serve from the left.

quiz.q: Under current BWF rules, the shuttle at service must be below…
quiz.why: BWF rules require the shuttle to be hit below 1.15 m from the court surface at service. A fixed height is easier to judge than the waist.

quiz.q: The singles court is…
quiz.why: The singles court is long and narrow: it uses the inner side lines, so it is narrower, but the full length. Doubles uses the full width.

lessons.title: Grips and the ready position

scenes.text: Wei, 10, in Singapore, holds his racket like a frying pan, face flat towards the net.
His backhand never reaches the back of the court.
His coach shows him the 'handshake' forehand grip and the thumb-up backhand grip.
Within a month his clears reach the back line from both sides.

steps.title: Forehand grip (the handshake)
steps.body:
- Hold the racket with the **frame edge facing you** (racket face perpendicular to the floor).
- 'Shake hands' with the handle: a **V** between thumb and index finger sits on the top-left bevel (for right-handers).
- Fingers slightly spread; index finger a little apart like a trigger.
- Hold **loosely** — tighten only at the moment of hitting for power.

steps.title: Backhand grip (thumb grip)
steps.body:
- From the forehand grip, turn the racket slightly so the **thumb pad sits flat on the wide back bevel** of the handle.
- The thumb pushes through the shuttle on backhand shots.
- Switch between forehand and backhand grips quickly using your fingers — practise this a lot.

steps.title: Ready position and the split step
steps.body:
- Stand near the **centre (base)** of your court, feet shoulder-width, knees bent, weight on the balls of the feet.
- Racket **up** in front of you.
- As the opponent hits, do a small **split step** (a little hop landing on both feet) so you can push off instantly in any direction.

steps.title: Common grip mistakes
steps.body:
- **Frying-pan grip**: no power on backhands and stiff wrist.
- **Squeezing too hard**: tires the forearm and reduces speed and touch; can contribute to elbow pain.
- Holding the racket too close to the head of the handle — hold it lower for reach and power (shorter for net play).

steps.title: Grip switch drill
steps.body: With a racket in hand, switch from forehand to backhand grip and back 20 times without looking, using only your fingers. Then shadow 10 forehand and 10 backhand swings, relaxing the grip between each.

activity.prompt: Grip & ready-position drill (10 minutes)
items: Check forehand handshake grip: V on the top-left bevel (right-hander)
Check backhand grip: thumb flat on the wide back bevel
20 grip switches without looking
10 split steps from the base, landing balanced
Shadow 10 forehand and 10 backhand swings with a relaxed grip
Shake out your forearm and wrist after the drill

quiz.q: The forehand grip is often called the…
quiz.why: The forehand grip is called the handshake grip because you hold the handle as if shaking hands with it. The frying-pan grip is a wrong, flat hold.

quiz.q: In the backhand grip, the thumb is…
options: Flat on the wide back bevel
quiz.why: In the backhand grip, the thumb lies flat on the wide back bevel of the handle. The thumb pad then pushes through the shot for power.

quiz.q: What is a split step?
options: A small hop landing on both feet as the opponent hits
quiz.why: A split step is a small hop that lands on both feet just as the opponent hits. It readies you to push off in any direction.

quiz.q: Why hold the racket loosely?
options: Faster swing and better touch; less forearm tension
quiz.why: A loose grip allows a faster swing and better touch, and it avoids tense forearms. You then squeeze at the moment of impact.

lessons.title: Footwork: moving to all six corners

scenes.text: Priyanka, 15, from Lucknow, can hit every shot — if she arrives in time. Mostly she doesn't.
Her coach marks six spots on the court and makes her 'shadow' to each and back to base.
She learns the chassé, the crossover, and the lunge with her racket leg forward.
Two months later she's reaching shots she'd have given up on.

steps.title: Six corners and the base
steps.body: Think of the court as **six target areas**: two at the net, two at the mid-court sides, two at the back. After every shot, **recover to the base** (roughly the centre of your court, slightly behind the middle in singles).

steps.title: Key steps
steps.body:
- **Split step** as the opponent hits.
- **Chassé**: a side-step where one foot chases the other without crossing — quick and balanced.
- **Crossover step** for longer distances.
- **Lunge** at the net and sides: step with the **racket-side leg forward** (right leg for right-handers), heel landing first, knee over the ankle (not beyond the toes), back leg extended for balance.
- **Recover**: push back from the lunge to the base.

steps.title: Moving to the back
steps.body: For a high shuttle to your forehand rear corner: turn sideways, use chassé steps back, get **behind the shuttle**, then hit with a scissor-kick (legs switch in the air) or a jump if appropriate, landing balanced. For the backhand rear corner, many players use a **round-the-head** forehand when possible because it's stronger than a backhand.

steps.title: Protect your knees and ankles
steps.body:
- Never let the knee collapse inward or go far beyond the toes when lunging.
- Wear **non-marking court shoes** with grip and cushioning — not running shoes.
- Warm up the ankles, knees and hips before playing.

General education, not medical advice. Persistent knee or ankle pain → see a doctor or physio.

steps.title: Shadow footwork drill
steps.body: A partner points randomly to one of the six corners. You move there, shadow a shot, and return to base. 12 movements per set, 3 sets, rest 1 minute between.

activity.prompt: Six-corner shadow footwork session
items: Warm-up: skipping 2 minutes, ankle rolls, hip circles, lunges
3 sets × 12 random six-corner movements with split step
Lunge check: racket leg forward, knee over ankle, heel first
Practise 10 chassé steps each side
Practise 5 scissor-kick landings at the rear court
Cool-down: calf, quad and hip-flexor stretches

quiz.q: In a lunge to the net (right-handed player), which leg goes forward?
quiz.why: A right-handed player lunges to the net with the right (racket-side) leg forward. This gives reach and balance for the stroke.

quiz.q: After each shot you should…
quiz.why: After each shot, recover to your base (near the centre). From there you can reach all four corners quickly.

quiz.q: A chassé is…
options: A side-step without crossing the feet
quiz.why: A chassé is a side-step where one foot chases the other without crossing. It is quick and keeps you balanced.

quiz.q: Which shoes suit badminton best?
quiz.why: Non-marking court shoes give grip and sideways support, and they do not leave marks on the floor. Running shoes slip sideways, and barefoot or slippers are unsafe.

lessons.title: The strokes: clear, drop, smash, net shot and serve

scenes.text: Anjali and Joel, 14, from Kochi, play doubles but only know one shot: hit hard.
Their coach teaches them: clear to push back, drop to bring forward, smash to finish, net shot to force a lift.
They start constructing rallies instead of hitting randomly.
They win their school championship — mostly with patient drops and sharp net kills.

steps.title: Overhead clear
steps.body:
- Turn **side-on**, non-racket arm up pointing at the shuttle, racket back.
- Hit the shuttle **high and in front** of you at full stretch.
- Rotate the trunk, forearm rotation (pronation) through contact; snap at impact.
- **Defensive clear**: high and deep to the back line, buying time. **Attacking clear**: flatter and faster over the opponent.

steps.title: Drop shot and smash
steps.body:
- **Drop**: same preparation as a clear (disguise!), but slow the racket at contact and guide the shuttle steeply just over the net.
- **Smash**: same preparation; hit the shuttle **in front** of the body, steeply downward, with full body rotation and forearm pronation. Use it when the shuttle is high and you're well-balanced, not from deep behind your body.
- Aim smashes at the opponent's body, the side lines, or the gap between doubles players.

steps.title: Net shot and lift
steps.body:
- **Net shot**: lunge in, racket up, gently **tumble or push** the shuttle just over the net so it falls close to the tape on the other side.
- **Lift**: from the net, push the shuttle high and deep to the back of the opponent's court when you can't play a net shot.
- Take the shuttle **as high as possible** at the net — the higher you meet it, the more options you have.

steps.title: The low serve
steps.body:
- Common in doubles and increasingly in singles: a short, flat serve that just clears the net and lands near the **short service line**.
- Backhand low serve: racket in front, short push with the thumb, shuttle below 1.15 m.
- The **high serve** (forehand, deep to the back line) is used in singles to push the opponent back.

steps.title: Common stroke mistakes
steps.body:
- Hitting overheads **behind the head** → weak shots and shoulder strain.
- Telegraphing the drop (obvious slow swing) → opponent reads it.
- Smashing every shuttle — you'll tire and become predictable.
- Not recovering to base after the shot.

activity.prompt: Match the stroke to its purpose.
pairs: High and deep to buy time
Steep and soft just over the net
Steep, fast attacking shot to finish
Tumbling close over the tape to force a lift
Pushing the shuttle high and deep from the net
Short, flat serve landing near the short service line

quiz.q: Why should the drop and the clear look the same at the start?
options: Disguise — the opponent can't read it
quiz.why: If the drop and the clear look the same at the start, the opponent cannot tell which shot is coming. This disguise delays their reaction.

quiz.q: Where should you contact the shuttle for a smash?
options: In front of the body, high
quiz.why: Hit the smash high and in front of the body. This gives a steep downward angle and lets you use your full swing. Behind the head makes it weak.

quiz.q: At the net, meet the shuttle…
quiz.why: At the net, meet the shuttle as high as possible. Higher contact gives more choices, such as a kill, and puts pressure on the opponent.

quiz.q: Which serve is most common in doubles?
quiz.why: In doubles, the low serve is most common. It stays low over the net, so the receiver cannot attack it easily.

quiz.q: A defensive clear aims…
options: High and deep to the back line
quiz.why: A defensive clear is hit high and deep to the back line. This gives you time to get back to base.

questions.q: Points to win a badminton game (normally)?
questions.why: A badminton game is normally played to 21 points, with a 2-point lead needed. 11 and 15 are older formats.

questions.q: A shuttle on the line is…
questions.why: In badminton the lines are in. A shuttle that lands on the line counts as in.

questions.q: The forehand grip is the…
questions.why: The forehand grip is the handshake grip. The frying-pan grip is a mistaken flat hold.

questions.q: Which shot is steep and fast to finish a rally?
questions.why: The smash is a steep, fast downward shot used to finish a rally. A clear is high and deep, and a lift is defensive.

questions.q: Even score in singles: serve from…
questions.why: With an even score, you serve from the right court. With an odd score, you serve from the left.

questions.q: Best of how many games in a match?
questions.why: A badminton match is best of three games. The first player to win two games wins.

questions.q: Which step is a side-step without crossing the feet?
questions.why: A chassé is the side-step in which the feet do not cross. It keeps you balanced while moving sideways.

questions.q: Lunging, the knee should be…
options: Over the ankle, not collapsing inward
questions.why: When lunging, the knee should be over the ankle and not collapse inward. This protects the knee joint.

questions.q: The doubles service court's back limit is…
options: The doubles long service line, 0.76 m inside the back line
questions.why: In doubles, the service court is wide but short. It ends at the doubles long service line, 0.76 m inside the back boundary line.

questions.q: Score 20–20 in a game. What's needed to win?
questions.why: At 20–20 you must win by 2 points. This continues up to the cap, where at 29–29 the next point wins (30 maximum).

questions.q: Why is a round-the-head forehand often preferred in the backhand rear corner?
options: It's usually stronger than a backhand from there
questions.why: In the backhand rear corner, a round-the-head forehand is usually stronger than a backhand overhead. It lets you use the full forehand swing. It is a choice, not a rule.

questions.q: Which service action is a fault?
options: Hitting the shuttle above 1.15 m from the surface
Hitting the base of the shuttle first
questions.why: The current BWF rule is that the shuttle must be hit below 1.15 m from the court surface at service. Hitting above that is a fault. Hitting the base of the shuttle first is how it is meant to be done.

questions.q: Telegraphing a drop shot means…
options: Making it obvious early so the opponent reads it
questions.why: Telegraphing a drop shot means making it obvious early, usually with a slower swing. The opponent can then read it and reach it easily. Good players disguise it.

lessons.title: Tennis scoring and rules

scenes.text: Mrs. Kapoor, 62, from Delhi, takes up tennis after retiring. 'Why is zero called love?' she laughs.
Her coach, Neil, explains: 15, 30, 40, game — and that the history of the names is debated.
She keeps score aloud every point until it becomes automatic.
Six months later she wins her first club doubles match 6–4, 7–6.

steps.title: Points and games
steps.body:
Points in a game go: **0 (love) → 15 → 30 → 40 → game**.

- At **40–40** it's **deuce**. The next point gives **advantage**; win it again to win the game. Lose it and it's back to deuce.
- The **server's score is said first**: '30–15' means the server has 30.
- Some formats use **no-ad** scoring: at deuce, the next point wins.

steps.title: Sets and tie-breaks
steps.body:
- A **set** is won by the first to **6 games** with a lead of **2** (6–4, 7–5).
- At **6–6**, most sets use a **tie-break**: first to **7 points** with a 2-point lead. In tie-breaks, points are counted normally (1, 2, 3…).
- Since 2022, all four Grand Slam tournaments play a **10-point tie-break** at 6–6 in the deciding set.
- Matches are best of 3 sets (or best of 5 in men's Grand Slam singles).

steps.title: Serving and play
steps.body:
- The server stands **behind the baseline**, between the centre mark and the side line, and serves **diagonally** into the opposite service box. The first point of each game is served from the **right (deuce) side**, then alternate.
- Two attempts: miss both = **double fault** (point lost).
- A serve that clips the net and lands in is a **let** — replayed.
- **Foot fault**: touching the baseline or court with a foot before hitting the ball.
- In a rally, the ball may bounce **once** (or be volleyed before it bounces). A ball touching any part of the line is **in**.
- Players change ends after the 1st, 3rd, 5th… game of each set.

steps.title: Etiquette
steps.body:
- Call the score clearly before serving.
- In matches without umpires, you call lines on **your side** — and if unsure, the ball is **in** for your opponent.
- Don't walk behind a court while a point is being played.

activity.prompt: Fill the tennis score sequence.
activity.text: Points go love, 15, ___, 40, game. At 40–40 it's called ___. Win the next point and you have ___.

quiz.q: What does 'love' mean in tennis scoring?
quiz.why: In tennis scoring, 'love' means zero. The points go love, 15, 30, 40.

quiz.q: At 6–6 in most sets, players play…
quiz.why: At 6–6 in a set, most tournaments use a tie-break. It is usually first to 7 points with a 2-point lead.

quiz.q: A serve hits the net and lands in the correct box. That's…
quiz.why: A serve that touches the net and lands in the correct service box is a let. It is replayed and is not a fault.

quiz.q: Two missed serves in a row is a…
quiz.why: Missing both serves in a row is a double fault, and the server loses the point.

quiz.q: Score '15–40' means…
quiz.why: The server's score is called first. So 15–40 means the server has 15 and the receiver has 40.

lessons.title: Tennis grips, groundstrokes, volley and serve

scenes.text: Kavya, 13, in Pune, hits her forehand with a flat wrist and a very late swing.
Her coach films it: no unit turn, no follow-through.
They practise 'turn, drop, swing, finish over the shoulder' with a semi-western grip.
Her forehand becomes her weapon — heavy topspin landing deep.

steps.title: The main grips
steps.body:
Picture the handle as an octagon with 8 bevels. The base knuckle of your index finger sits on a different bevel for each grip.

- **Continental** ('hammer grip'): used for **serves, volleys, overheads and slices**.
- **Eastern forehand** ('shake hands with the racket'): good for flatter forehands.
- **Semi-western**: hand turned further under the handle — good for **topspin** forehands; very common today.
- **Backhand**: one-handed (eastern backhand) or two-handed (dominant hand continental, other hand eastern forehand above it).

steps.title: Groundstrokes: forehand and backhand
steps.body:
1. **Ready position**, split step as the opponent hits.
2. **Unit turn**: turn shoulders and hips early, racket back.
3. **Move** to the ball and set your feet.
4. **Swing low to high** for topspin, contacting the ball **in front** of the body around waist height.
5. **Follow through** — over the shoulder for a forehand.
6. **Recover** to the centre of the baseline.

steps.title: Volley
steps.body:
- Continental grip, racket up in front.
- **Short punch**, no big backswing; step forward into the ball.
- Firm wrist; contact in front of the body.

steps.title: The serve
steps.body:
- Continental grip; side-on stance behind the baseline.
- **Toss** slightly in front and towards your hitting side, high enough to hit at full stretch. A consistent toss is the foundation of a consistent serve.
- **Trophy position**: tossing arm up, racket back, knees bent.
- Drive up through the ball, pronating the forearm, and follow through across the body.
- Beginners can start with a simpler 'abbreviated' motion and add rhythm later.

steps.title: Avoiding tennis elbow and shoulder strain
steps.body:
- Squeezing the grip too hard and late, arm-only swings, and a heavy or badly strung racket can contribute to **lateral elbow pain** ('tennis elbow').
- Use the **legs and trunk**, not just the arm. Warm up the shoulder.
- Persistent pain → rest and see a doctor or physiotherapist. General education, not medical advice.

activity.prompt: Order the forehand groundstroke.
