Unit turn: shoulders and hips rotate, racket back
Move and set your feet
Swing low to high, contact in front of the body
Follow through over the shoulder
Recover to the centre of the baseline

quiz.q: Which grip is used for serves and volleys?
quiz.why: The continental grip is used for serves and volleys, because it lets you change the racket angle easily. Western or semi-western grips suit heavy topspin groundstrokes.

quiz.q: For topspin, the swing goes…
quiz.why: For topspin, you swing low to high, brushing up the back of the ball. This makes it spin forward and dip.

quiz.q: A volley should have…
options: A short punch with a firm wrist
quiz.why: A volley is a short punch with a firm wrist, with the racket in front. A big backswing gives too little time at the net.

quiz.q: The foundation of a consistent serve is…
quiz.why: A consistent toss is the foundation of a consistent serve. If the ball goes to a different place each time, the serve will vary too.

lessons.title: Table tennis: rules and the legal serve

scenes.text: Ritika, 11, plays table tennis at her community centre in Chennai, hiding the ball behind her hand on serves.
At a local tournament, the umpire calls her serve illegal.
Her coach teaches her the service law: open palm, toss at least 16 cm, ball visible.
Her new legal serve is just as tricky — and she reaches the semi-final.

steps.title: The table and ball
steps.body:
- Table: **2.74 m long, 1.525 m wide, 76 cm high**.
- Net: **15.25 cm** high.
- Ball: **40 mm** diameter (plastic in modern competitions).
- Racket: the two sides must have different colours — one **black**, the other a bright contrasting colour (traditionally red).

steps.title: Scoring
steps.body:
- A game is won by the first to **11 points** with a **2-point lead**.
- Matches are best of an odd number of games (e.g., best of 5 or 7).
- **Service changes every 2 points**. At **10–10**, each player serves **one point** in turn until someone leads by 2.
- Players change ends after each game, and in the last possible game when someone reaches 5 points.

steps.title: The legal serve
steps.body:
- The ball starts resting on your **open, flat, stationary palm**.
- Toss it **near-vertically upwards at least 16 cm**, without spin, and hit it as it **falls**.
- From the start of the serve until it's struck, the ball must be **above the level of the playing surface** and **behind your end line**.
- The ball must **not be hidden** from the receiver by your body or arm.
- It must bounce **once on your side**, then **once on the receiver's side**.
- In singles, you can serve anywhere on the receiver's side. In **doubles**, serve **diagonally from your right half to the receiver's right half**.
- If the serve touches the net and is otherwise good, it's a **let** — replayed.

steps.title: Common faults
steps.body:
- Tossing from cupped fingers or throwing the ball sideways.
- Hiding the contact with your free arm or body.
- Volleying the ball before it bounces on your side (in a rally that's a lost point).
- Touching the table with your free hand, or moving the table, during a rally.

statements.s: A table tennis game is played to 11 points with a 2-point lead.
statements.why: Yes — first to 11, win by 2.

statements.s: Service changes every 5 points.
statements.why: Every 2 points; every point at 10–10.

statements.s: The ball must be tossed at least 16 cm on a serve.
statements.why: Required by the service law.

statements.s: In doubles, the serve goes from the server's right half to the receiver's right half.
statements.why: Diagonal right-to-right.

statements.s: You may hide the ball from the receiver during the serve.
statements.why: The ball must be visible to the receiver.

quiz.q: At 10–10, how is service arranged?
options: Each player serves one point in turn
quiz.why: At 10–10 in table tennis, each player serves one point in turn. This continues until someone leads by 2 points.

quiz.q: How high must the serve toss be at least?
quiz.why: In table tennis the ball must be thrown up at least 16 cm after leaving the palm. Lower tosses are not allowed.

quiz.q: Where must the ball be during the serve?
options: Behind the end line and above the playing surface
quiz.why: During the serve, the ball must be behind the end line and above the playing surface. It is visible to the receiver at all times.

quiz.q: A serve clips the net and lands correctly. That's…
quiz.why: A serve that clips the net and lands correctly is a let, so it is replayed. It is not a fault and not a point.

lessons.title: Table tennis grips, strokes and spin

scenes.text: Mr. Sharma, 70, from Indore, has played table tennis every morning for 40 years.
His grandson Dev, 12, hits hard but every return from grandpa comes back with heavy backspin into the net.
Grandpa explains: 'Read the spin. Open your bat to lift backspin. Brush up for topspin.'
A month later Dev loops grandpa's chop for a winner. They both cheer.

steps.title: Grips
steps.body:
- **Shakehand**: like shaking hands — thumb and index finger on either side of the blade, other fingers around the handle. Balanced for forehand and backhand; most common.
- **Penhold**: held like a pen, popular in parts of Asia; strong forehand and wrist play, backhand techniques vary.
- Keep the grip **relaxed**; the **neutral** grip (no strong forehand or backhand bias) is best for beginners.

steps.title: Understanding spin
steps.body:
- **Topspin**: bat brushes **up** the back of the ball; the ball dips down and kicks forward after the bounce. To return it, **close** the bat face (angle it forward).
- **Backspin (underspin)**: bat brushes **under** the ball; the ball floats and checks. To return it, **open** the bat face (angle it back) and lift.
- **Sidespin**: bat brushes the side; the ball curves and kicks sideways.

Watch the **opponent's bat movement** to read spin.

steps.title: The four basic strokes
steps.body:
- **Forehand drive (counter-hit)**: small backswing, rotate waist, bat closed, brush slightly forward-upward, finish near the forehead.
- **Backhand drive**: bat in front of the body, elbow forward, flick forward from the elbow and forearm.
- **Push**: a short, controlled backspin stroke against backspin — open bat, push forward and under.
- **Block**: against fast topspin attacks — short stroke, bat angle closed, use the opponent's pace.

Then the **loop** (heavy topspin attack) builds on the drive.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swinging with the arm only — use the **waist and legs**.
- Standing too close or too far from the table (about an arm's length plus a bit is a common starting point).
- Not watching the opponent's bat → misreading spin.
- Big backswings — table tennis rewards compact strokes.

steps.title: Drill: rally counter
steps.body: With a partner, rally forehand-to-forehand diagonally. Count your longest rally. Then backhand-to-backhand. Then one player pushes, the other pushes back. Aim for 50-ball rallies.

activity.prompt: Match the spin to how you return it.
pairs: Open the bat face and lift
Short stroke using the opponent's pace

quiz.q: Which grip is most common worldwide?
quiz.why: Shakehand is the most common grip worldwide. You hold the bat as if shaking hands. Penhold is used by fewer players.

quiz.q: To return heavy backspin, you should…
quiz.why: Backspin makes the ball drop, so it goes into the net if you hit it flat. Open the bat face and lift it to counter the spin.

quiz.q: Topspin makes the ball…
options: Dip and kick forward after the bounce
quiz.why: Topspin makes the ball dip down quickly and then kick forward after the bounce. Backspin makes the ball float and check.

quiz.q: How do you read spin?
quiz.why: The opponent's bat movement tells you the spin. For example, a brush upward means topspin, and a brush under means backspin.

questions.q: Tennis: zero is called…
questions.why: In tennis, zero is called 'love'.

questions.q: Table tennis game is played to…
questions.why: A table tennis game is played to 11 points (win by 2).

questions.q: Which grip suits serves and volleys in tennis?
questions.why: The continental grip suits serves and volleys. The western grip is for heavy topspin on groundstrokes.

questions.q: Tennis: 40–40 is…
questions.why: When both players have 40, the score is called deuce. A player must then win two points in a row.

questions.q: How often does service change in table tennis (before 10–10)?
questions.why: In table tennis the serve changes every 2 points until 10–10, after which it changes every point.

questions.q: Topspin swing path in tennis is…
questions.why: Topspin is hit with a low-to-high swing, brushing up and over the back of the ball.

questions.q: A tennis set at 6–6 usually goes to…
questions.why: At 6–6 in a set, play usually goes to a tie-break. Playing on to 8 games would not be a standard rule.

questions.q: Minimum table tennis serve toss?
questions.why: The ball must be thrown up at least 16 cm in table tennis, to stop hidden or flat serves.

questions.q: Return of heavy backspin in table tennis needs…
questions.why: Backspin makes the ball drop, so you need an open bat to lift it. A closed bat sends it into the net.

questions.q: In a standard tie-break, the winner is first to…
questions.why: A standard tie-break is first to 7 points with a 2-point lead. Grand Slam deciding sets now use a 10-point tie-break instead.

questions.q: In table tennis doubles, the serve must go…
options: From server's right half to receiver's right half
questions.why: In table tennis doubles, the serve must go diagonally from the server's right half to the receiver's right half. It cannot go anywhere else.

questions.q: Since 2022, Grand Slam deciding sets at 6–6 use…
questions.why: Since 2022 the Grand Slam deciding sets use a 10-point tie-break at 6–6. This ends the very long advantage sets.

questions.q: Why must the ball stay visible during a table tennis serve?
options: So the receiver can read the spin; hiding it is illegal
questions.why: The ball must stay visible so the receiver can read the spin. Hiding it with the body or arm is illegal.

lessons.title: Sprinting: starts, mechanics and relays

scenes.text: Sunita, 14, the fastest girl in her school in Patiala, flinches before the gun at the district meet.
She's disqualified — one false start and you're out.
Her coach teaches her to focus on the sound, not to guess, and to practise 'set' holds.
At the next meet she waits for the gun, explodes out, and wins the 100 m.

steps.title: The crouch start
steps.body:
- **'On your marks'**: feet in the blocks (front foot about 1.5–2 foot-lengths behind the line, back foot further back), knee of the back leg on the ground, hands just behind the line, shoulder-width apart, fingers bridged, arms straight.
- **'Set'**: raise the hips slightly above the shoulders, shoulders over or slightly ahead of the hands, weight forward, still.
- **Gun**: drive powerfully from both legs, the back leg swinging through first; arms pump hard; stay low for the first several strides, rising gradually.

steps.title: False starts
steps.body: Under World Athletics rules, **one false start leads to disqualification** in most events. Starting blocks with sensors treat a reaction faster than **0.100 seconds** after the gun as a false start, because humans can't genuinely react that fast. Moving after 'Set' but before the gun also counts.

steps.title: Sprint mechanics
steps.body:
- Run **tall** at top speed, slight forward lean from the ankles.
- Land on the **balls of the feet**, under the hips, not far in front.
- **High knee drive**, heel coming up under the hip.
- **Arms** swing forward and back (not across the body), elbows about 90°, hands relaxed (cheek to hip).
- **Relax** the face and shoulders — tension slows you down.

steps.title: Relay baton exchange (4×100 m)
steps.body:
- The baton must be passed **within the marked changeover zone** (30 m in current rules for the 4×100); where the baton is, not the runners, decides.
- The incoming runner shouts a signal ('Hand!'); the outgoing runner, already accelerating from a check mark, puts a hand back.
- **Upsweep** (hand low, baton pushed up) or **downsweep** (hand high, baton pushed down into a palm-up hand).
- Runners usually alternate hands so they stay on the inside or outside of the lane appropriately.
- Practise again and again — exchanges win or lose relays.

steps.title: Try this: drills
steps.body: A-skips (high knee skipping), B-skips, high knees, butt kicks, 3 × 20 m from a crouch start, and 4 × 30 m flying sprints (jog in 20 m, sprint 30 m). Walk back for full recovery — sprint training is about **quality**, not exhaustion.

activity.prompt: Put the sprint start in order.
items: Starter says 'On your marks'
Feet in blocks, back knee down, hands behind the line
Starter says 'Set'
Raise hips slightly above shoulders and hold still
Gun fires
Drive out low, back leg through first, arms pumping
Rise gradually to upright running

quiz.q: How many false starts lead to disqualification under World Athletics rules (most events)?
quiz.why: In most events under World Athletics rules, one false start gets the athlete disqualified. There are no warnings for each runner.

quiz.q: A reaction faster than what time is treated as a false start?
quiz.why: A reaction faster than 0.100 s after the gun is treated as a false start. It is too fast to be a real response to the sound, so the runner must have anticipated.

quiz.q: Sprinters' arms should swing…
quiz.why: Sprinters swing their arms forward and back, not across the body. This keeps the body running in a straight line.

quiz.q: In a relay, what decides if the exchange is legal?
options: Where the baton is when passed
quiz.why: A relay exchange is judged by where the baton is when it is passed, which must be inside the zone. The runners' feet positions do not decide it.

quiz.q: Sprint training should focus on…
quiz.why: Sprint training should be high quality with full recovery. Fast, well-rested reps develop speed, while tired running slows you down.

lessons.title: Middle and long distance: pacing and training

scenes.text: Kiprono, 16, runs at a school in Eldoret, Kenya. He loves to sprint the first lap of the 1500 m — and fade badly.
His coach gives him a stopwatch and target lap times.
He learns to run even laps and save something for the last 300 m.
He wins the county final, passing three runners on the last bend.

steps.title: Pacing
steps.body:
- **Even pace**: similar lap times throughout — efficient for most runners.
- **Negative split**: second half slightly faster than the first — a strong strategy for longer races.
- Starting too fast builds fatigue early and you slow down a lot.

On a standard **400 m track**, a 1600 m run is **4 laps**; the 1500 m is 3¾ laps.

steps.title: Worked example: lap targets
steps.body: Goal: 1600 m in 8 minutes (480 seconds). That's 4 laps → **120 seconds (2:00) per lap**, or 60 seconds per 200 m. Check at every lap; if you're at 1:50, ease off slightly; if 2:10, gradually pick it up.

steps.title: Building endurance safely
steps.body:
- **Easy runs** (most of your running): at a pace where you can talk in sentences.
- **Intervals**: e.g., 6 × 400 m at goal race pace with 90 s rest.
- **Tempo runs**: 15–20 min at 'comfortably hard'.
- **Increase weekly distance gradually**; a common rule of thumb is no more than about 10% a week.
- Rest days and sleep let the body adapt.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Consult a doctor before starting if you have heart, lung or other conditions. Stop and get help for chest pain, fainting or unusual breathlessness. Avoid hard running in extreme heat; hydrate. Pain that changes how you run (limping) → stop and get it checked. Emergency: **112**.

activity.prompt: You want to run 2400 m (6 laps of a 400 m track) in 12 minutes at even pace. How many seconds per lap?

quiz.q: A negative split means…
options: Second half faster than the first
quiz.why: A negative split means running the second half faster than the first. It is an efficient way to pace a race.

quiz.q: How many laps of a 400 m track make 1600 m?
quiz.why: 1600 m ÷ 400 m per lap = 4 laps.

quiz.q: Most of a distance runner's training should be…
quiz.why: Most distance training should be easy, conversational running. This builds the aerobic base safely, and hard sessions are only a small part.

quiz.q: A common rule of thumb for increasing weekly distance is…
quiz.why: A common rule of thumb is to increase weekly distance by about 10% a week. Gradual rises reduce the risk of injury.

lessons.title: Jumping: long jump and high jump basics

scenes.text: Neel, 13, from Thiruvananthapuram, jumps far — but his first three attempts are all no-jumps.
His coach measures his run-up from the board backwards and marks a check point.
He practises hitting the board without looking down.
In the final, his first legal jump wins the bronze medal.

steps.title: Long jump phases
steps.body:
1. **Approach**: a consistent, accelerating run-up (beginners often use 8–12 strides; experienced jumpers longer). Measure it from the board and mark it.
2. **Take-off**: from **one foot** on the board, driving the opposite knee and arms upward; head up, eyes forward.
3. **Flight**: hold a balanced position (sail, hang or hitch-kick techniques).
4. **Landing**: extend legs forward, then fall forward or sideways — **not back**.

steps.title: Long jump rules
steps.body:
- It's a **foul (no-jump)** if any part of the take-off foot goes **beyond the take-off line** (the front edge of the board).
- The jump is measured from the **take-off line** to the **nearest mark in the sand** made by any part of the body.
- So falling backwards after landing loses distance.

steps.title: High jump basics
steps.body:
- Take-off from **one foot** (two-foot take-offs are not allowed).
- Modern technique is the **Fosbury flop**: a **curved (J-shaped) approach**, take-off from the foot further from the bar, rotate to go over **back-first**, and land on the shoulders/upper back on a **proper landing mat**.
- Beginners can learn the **scissors** technique first.
- Three consecutive failures at a height eliminate you.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body:
- **Never attempt the flop without a proper high-jump landing mat.**
- Dig and rake the long jump pit before jumping; check it for stones or glass.
- Warm up thoroughly; jumps stress the ankles, knees and hamstrings.

statements.s: In the long jump, stepping beyond the take-off line is a foul.
statements.why: Any part of the take-off foot beyond the line = no-jump.

statements.s: Long jump is measured to the furthest mark you make.
statements.why: To the nearest mark made by any part of the body.

statements.s: High jumpers may take off from two feet.
statements.why: Take-off must be from one foot.

statements.s: You may practise the Fosbury flop onto grass if you're careful.
statements.why: Always use a proper landing mat.

statements.s: Falling backwards after landing can cost distance in long jump.
statements.why: The mark nearest the board is measured.

quiz.q: Long jump distance is measured to…
options: The nearest mark in the sand made by any part of the body
quiz.why: In the long jump, the distance is measured to the nearest mark in the sand made by any part of the body. So falling backwards after landing can cost distance.

quiz.q: High jump take-off must be from…
quiz.why: In the high jump, the take-off must be from one foot. Two-foot take-offs are not allowed.

quiz.q: The Fosbury flop uses which approach?
quiz.why: The Fosbury flop uses a curved (J-shaped) approach. The curve helps the jumper turn their back to the bar.

quiz.q: How many consecutive failures eliminate a high jumper?
quiz.why: A high jumper is eliminated after three consecutive failures, at any height or combination of heights.

lessons.title: Throwing: shot put technique and throwing safety

scenes.text: At a school sports day in Bhopal, a student walks across the throwing area to fetch a lost bottle.
Coach Rekha blows her whistle — a shot has just landed two metres away from him.
She stops the event and teaches everyone the throwing-area rules.
For the rest of the day, no one enters the sector without her signal. Everyone is safe.

steps.title: Throwing-area safety first
steps.body:
- **Never enter** or cross a throwing sector while throwing is in progress.
- Throw only when the coach/official signals the area is **clear**.
- **Retrieve implements only on signal**, all together; **carry** them back — never throw them back.
- Stand behind the thrower, never in front or to the side close by.
- Use the correct implement weight for your age.

steps.title: Shot put basics (standing put)
steps.body:
- Hold the shot at the **base of the fingers** (not the palm), fingers slightly spread, thumb for support.
- Place it against the **neck under the jaw**, elbow up and out.
- Stand side-on at the back of the circle, weight on the back leg, knees bent.
- **Drive** the hips round and up, then **push** the shot away from the neck at about 35–40° with the arm, finishing with a flick of the fingers.
- It's a **put** (push), not a throw: the shot must not drop below the shoulder line or go behind it during the put.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- The circle is **2.135 m** in diameter, with a **stop board** at the front.
- A put is a foul if you touch the top of the stop board or the ground outside the circle, or leave the circle before the shot lands; you must **exit from the rear half**.
- The shot must land within the sector lines.
- Senior men's shot is **7.26 kg**; senior women's **4 kg**; youth shots are lighter.

steps.title: Progressions
steps.body: Beginners learn the **standing put**, then the **glide** (moving backwards across the circle) or **rotational** technique (spinning, like a discus thrower). Strength in the legs and core matters more than arm strength.

activity.prompt: Throwing session safety checklist
items: Check the throwing sector is clear and marked
Agree whistle signals: 'throw' and 'retrieve'
Everyone stands behind the thrower
Use the correct shot weight for age
Hold the shot at the base of the fingers against the neck
Put (push) — never throw it like a ball
Retrieve together on signal and carry implements back

quiz.q: How should you return a shot after a put?
options: Carry it back on the signal
quiz.why: After a put, the shot is carried back, not thrown or rolled. This is the safe rule, so no one is hit by a heavy implement.

quiz.q: Where is the shot held?
options: At the base of the fingers against the neck
quiz.why: The shot is held at the base of the fingers, against the neck. It is not held in the palm.

quiz.q: From which part of the circle must you exit after a put?
quiz.why: After the put, you must leave the circle from the rear half. Leaving from the front is a foul.

quiz.q: Shot put is a 'put' because…
options: It is hit with a bat
It is pushed from the shoulder, not thrown
quiz.why: The shot is 'put', not thrown, because it must be pushed from the neck and shoulder. Throwing it is not allowed.

questions.q: Commands at a sprint start are…
questions.why: The official sprint start commands are 'On your marks', 'Set', and then the gun.

questions.q: A shot is returned by…
questions.why: The shot is always carried back after a put. It is never thrown.

questions.q: How many laps of a 400 m track make 800 m?
questions.why: 800 m ÷ 400 m per lap = 2 laps.

questions.q: Long jump foul happens when…
options: Foot goes beyond the take-off line
questions.why: A long jump foul is when the foot goes beyond the take-off line. The attempt is a no-jump and is not measured.

questions.q: Sprinters land on…
questions.why: Sprinters land on the balls of the feet, under the hips. Landing on the heels would slow them down.

questions.q: High jump take-off is from…
questions.why: The high jump take-off must be from one foot.

questions.q: Goal: 1600 m in 6:40. Seconds per lap at even pace?
questions.why: 6:40 is 400 seconds. Over 4 laps, an even pace is 400 ÷ 4 = 100 seconds per lap.

questions.q: Long jump is measured to…
options: Nearest mark made by the body
questions.why: A long jump is measured to the nearest mark made by the body, not the furthest one.

questions.q: Baton legality depends on…
questions.why: A relay exchange is legal if the baton is passed within the zone. The position of the baton decides it, not the feet.

questions.q: What is wrong with sprinting the first lap of a 1500 m flat out?
options: Early fatigue makes you slow a lot later
questions.why: Sprinting the first lap flat out causes early fatigue, so you slow a lot later. Even or negative splits are more efficient.

questions.q: Shot put diameter of circle?
questions.why: The shot put circle has a diameter of 2.135 m.

questions.q: Why is a reaction under 0.100 s treated as a false start?
options: It's faster than humans can genuinely react to the sound
questions.why: A reaction under 0.100 s is faster than a human can genuinely react to the sound. That shows the runner started before hearing the gun, which is anticipation.

questions.q: Senior men's shot weighs…
questions.why: The senior men's shot weighs 7.26 kg (16 lb). 5 kg and 4 kg are lighter youth or women's weights.

lessons.title: What yoga is, and how to practise safely

scenes.text: Emma, 30, from Melbourne, comes to Varanasi expecting yoga to be about bending as far as possible.
Her teacher, Shri Raghunath, spends the first class on breathing, sitting still and kindness to her own body.
He explains that asanas are just one of the eight limbs described by Patanjali.
By the end of the month Emma feels calmer than ever — and her hamstrings are looser too.

steps.title: Yoga is more than poses
steps.body:
The *Yoga Sutras of Patanjali* define yoga as the stilling of the fluctuations of the mind (*yogaś citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ*, Sutra 1.2). Patanjali describes **eight limbs (ashtanga)**:

1. **Yama** — ethical restraints (e.g., non-violence, truthfulness).
2. **Niyama** — personal observances (e.g., cleanliness, contentment).
3. **Asana** — steady, comfortable posture.
4. **Pranayama** — breath regulation.
5. **Pratyahara** — withdrawal of the senses.
6. **Dharana** — concentration.
7. **Dhyana** — meditation.
8. **Samadhi** — absorption.

The UN declared **21 June** as the **International Day of Yoga** (first observed in 2015).

steps.title: Safety first
steps.body:
This is general education, not medical advice. **Consult a doctor before starting if you have high blood pressure, heart disease, glaucoma or eye problems, back or neck problems, recent surgery, are pregnant, or have any chronic condition.** Pregnant learners should follow a qualified prenatal yoga teacher.

- **Never force** a pose. Mild stretch is good; pain is a stop sign.
- Avoid inversions and strong breath-holding if you have uncontrolled high blood pressure or glaucoma.
- Stop if you feel dizzy, numb or breathless.

steps.title: Practical guidelines
steps.body:
- Practise on an **empty or light stomach** — wait about 2–3 hours after a heavy meal.
- Use a **non-slip mat** on a flat surface; comfortable clothes.
- **Breathe through the nose** steadily; never hold your breath in poses unless instructed.
- Move **slowly** into and out of poses.
- Use props — a folded blanket, cushion, wall or chair — they are tools, not 'cheating'.
- End with **Shavasana** (relaxation).

steps.title: The Common Yoga Protocol
steps.body: India's Ministry of Ayush publishes a **Common Yoga Protocol** — a short, standardised sequence of loosening practices, asanas, pranayama and meditation suitable for most people, used on International Day of Yoga. It's a good, free starting point.

activity.prompt: Match each limb of yoga to its meaning.

quiz.q: How many limbs of yoga does Patanjali describe?
quiz.why: Patanjali describes eight limbs of yoga (Ashtanga, from ashta = eight). Asana, the postures, is only one of them.

quiz.q: International Day of Yoga is on…
quiz.why: International Day of Yoga is on 21 June. The United Nations declared it, after a proposal by India.

quiz.q: Pain during a pose means…
quiz.why: Pain in a pose is a warning sign. Stop or ease off. Pushing through pain can cause injury.

quiz.q: How long should you wait after a heavy meal?
quiz.why: Wait about 2–3 hours after a heavy meal before yoga. Practising on a light or empty stomach is more comfortable.

quiz.q: Props like blankets and chairs are…
quiz.why: Props like blankets, blocks and chairs are helpful tools. They make poses safer and more accessible, so using them is not cheating.

sources: Ministry of Ayush — Common Yoga Protocol

lessons.title: Standing asanas: Tadasana, Vrikshasana, Trikonasana, Virabhadrasana

scenes.text: Arjun, 11, from Mysuru, keeps falling out of Vrikshasana (tree pose) in school yoga.
His teacher tells him to fix his gaze on one point on the wall — a drishti.
She also lets him rest his foot on his calf instead of his thigh.
Arjun holds the tree for 30 seconds. 'Balance starts in the mind,' says his teacher.

steps.title: Tadasana (mountain pose)
steps.body:
- Stand with feet together or hip-width, weight even across both feet.
- Thighs gently engaged, tailbone lengthening down, belly soft.
- Shoulders relaxed down, arms by your sides (or raised overhead in the common variation).
- Crown of the head lifting; breathe steadily.

It teaches **posture and awareness** — the base of all standing poses.

steps.title: Vrikshasana (tree pose)
steps.body:
- From Tadasana, shift weight to the left foot.
- Place the right sole on the inner **left calf or inner thigh — never on the knee joint**.
- Hands in prayer at the chest or raised overhead.
- Fix your **gaze** on a still point. Hold 20–30 seconds; switch sides.

**Modify**: toes on the floor with heel on the ankle, or use a wall for support.

steps.title: Trikonasana (triangle pose)
steps.body:
- Step feet wide (about a leg's length). Turn the right foot out 90°, left foot slightly in.
- Arms out at shoulder height. Reach right, then hinge at the **hip** (not the waist) and lower the right hand to the shin, ankle or a block; left arm up.
- Keep both sides of the waist long; chest open. Look up, forward or down — whatever is comfortable for your neck.

**Caution**: with neck problems, look down; with low blood pressure, come up slowly.

steps.title: Virabhadrasana II (warrior II)
steps.body:
- Feet wide; right foot out 90°, left foot slightly in.
- Bend the right knee to about 90°, **knee over the ankle**, tracking towards the second/third toe.
- Arms out at shoulder height; gaze over the front hand.
- Torso upright, shoulders relaxed. Hold 20–30 s; switch sides.

**Common mistake**: the knee collapsing inward or going far past the ankle.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Practise the four poses in sequence, holding each for 5 slow breaths per side. Notice which side is harder — that's normal, and practice evens it out.

statements.s: In Vrikshasana, place the foot on the side of the knee joint.
statements.why: Never on the knee — on the calf or inner thigh.

statements.s: Fixing your gaze on a still point helps balance.
statements.why: A drishti steadies balance.

statements.s: In Trikonasana, you hinge at the hip rather than collapsing at the waist.
statements.why: That keeps both sides of the waist long.

statements.s: In Warrior II, the front knee should cave inward.
statements.why: It should track over the ankle toward the second/third toe.

statements.s: Using a wall in tree pose is allowed.
statements.why: Support is a valid modification.

quiz.q: Where should the foot NOT be placed in Vrikshasana?
options: On the ankle with toes down
quiz.why: In Vrikshasana (tree pose), the foot goes on the ankle, calf or inner thigh, but not on the knee joint. Pressing on the knee can strain it.

quiz.q: Which pose is the foundation of standing poses?
quiz.why: Tadasana (mountain pose) is the foundation of standing poses. It teaches the basic alignment and balance used in other standing poses.

quiz.q: In Warrior II, the front knee should be…
quiz.why: In Warrior II, the front knee should stay over the ankle. If it moves past the ankle or caves in, it can strain the knee.

quiz.q: With neck problems in Trikonasana, you might…
quiz.why: With neck problems, in Trikonasana you can look down instead of up at the raised hand. This avoids straining the neck.

lessons.title: Seated and lying asanas: Bhujangasana, Balasana, Setu Bandhasana, Paschimottanasana, Shavasana

scenes.text: Neha, 27, a call-centre worker in Noida, has a stiff back after night shifts.
Her doctor rules out anything serious and suggests gentle movement, including yoga.
She learns a gentle cobra, child's pose and bridge — and to skip deep forward bends for now.
Ten minutes after each shift, her back feels looser and she sleeps better.

steps.title: Bhujangasana (cobra)
steps.body:
- Lie on your stomach, legs together, tops of the feet on the floor.
- Hands under the shoulders, elbows close to the body.
- Inhale and lift the head and chest **using your back muscles**, keeping the lower ribs near the floor at first; elbows stay bent.
- Shoulders away from the ears; gaze forward.
- Hold for a few breaths, exhale down.

**Caution**: avoid or keep very low with back injury, during pregnancy, or after abdominal surgery.

steps.title: Balasana (child's pose)
steps.body:
- Kneel, big toes together, knees together or apart.
- Sit back towards the heels and fold forward, forehead on the floor or a cushion.
- Arms forward or alongside the body. Breathe into the back.

A **resting pose**. Place a cushion between thighs and calves if knees are uncomfortable.

steps.title: Setu Bandhasana (bridge)
steps.body:
- Lie on your back, knees bent, feet hip-width flat on the floor near the hips.
- Arms by your sides, palms down.
- Press into the feet and lift the hips; keep knees in line with the feet.
- Keep the **neck still** — don't turn your head while lifted.
- Hold 5 breaths; roll down slowly.

steps.title: Paschimottanasana (seated forward bend)
steps.body:
- Sit with legs straight forward (sit on a folded blanket if your back rounds).
- Inhale, lengthen the spine; exhale and **hinge from the hips**, reaching for shins, ankles or a strap around the feet.
- Keep the back as long as you can; bend the knees if needed.

**Caution**: people with disc problems or acute back pain should avoid deep forward bends unless cleared by a doctor or physio. Those with osteoporosis should avoid loaded spinal flexion.

steps.title: Shavasana (corpse pose / relaxation)
steps.body:
- Lie on your back, legs slightly apart, arms a little away from the body, palms up.
- Close your eyes; let the breath become natural.
- Scan from toes to head, relaxing each part.
- Stay 5–10 minutes. Roll to the right side and sit up slowly.

A cushion under the knees helps the lower back.

cards.back: Cobra: lift chest with back muscles, elbows bent; caution with back injury, pregnancy.
Child's pose: a resting fold; cushion for the knees if needed.
Bridge: lift hips, knees in line with feet, don't turn the neck.
Seated forward bend: hinge from hips; avoid deep bends with disc problems.
Relaxation lying on the back, 5–10 minutes; come out via the right side.

quiz.q: In Bhujangasana, the lift should come mainly from…
quiz.why: In Bhujangasana (cobra), the lift should come from the back muscles with the elbows bent. Pushing hard on straight arms can overload the lower back.

quiz.q: Why not turn your head in Setu Bandhasana?
quiz.why: In Setu Bandhasana (bridge), the weight is on the shoulders and neck. Turning the head can strain the neck, so keep it still.

quiz.q: Who should avoid deep forward bends unless cleared?
options: People with disc problems or acute back pain
quiz.why: People with disc problems or acute back pain should avoid deep forward bends unless cleared by a doctor. Bending the spine forward can aggravate a disc.

quiz.q: How do you come out of Shavasana?
options: Roll to the side and sit up slowly
quiz.why: Come out of Shavasana slowly by rolling to one side and then sitting up. Moving too quickly can cause dizziness.

lessons.title: Surya Namaskar (sun salutation)

scenes.text: Mr. and Mrs. Joshi, both 48, in Pune, decide to do Surya Namaskar on their terrace every morning.
On day one they rush 12 rounds and feel dizzy.
A yoga teacher at their society shows them to go slow, breathe with each movement and start with 3 rounds.
Six months later, they do 10 calm rounds daily — and their evening walks feel easier.

steps.title: The 12 positions (one common sequence)
steps.body:
Several versions exist; this is a widely taught one. Breathe with each movement.

1. **Pranamasana** (prayer) — exhale.
2. **Hasta Uttanasana** (raised arms) — inhale.
3. **Padahastasana** (standing forward bend) — exhale.
4. **Ashwa Sanchalanasana** (lunge, right leg back) — inhale.
5. **Parvatasana** (mountain/inverted V; some versions use plank, Dandasana) — exhale.
6. **Ashtanga Namaskara** (knees, chest, chin to floor) — hold out or natural breath.
7. **Bhujangasana** (cobra) — inhale.
8. **Parvatasana** — exhale.
9. **Ashwa Sanchalanasana** (right leg forward) — inhale.
10. **Padahastasana** — exhale.
11. **Hasta Uttanasana** — inhale.
12. **Pranamasana** — exhale.

Repeat leading with the other leg to complete one full round.

steps.title: How to practise
steps.body:
- Start with **2–3 slow rounds**, adding gradually.
- **Bend the knees** in the forward bend if your hamstrings are tight.
- Lower the back knee to the floor in the lunge.
- In Ashtanga Namaskara, lower carefully; skip it and lie flat if needed.
- Move with the breath; never hold it strenuously.
- Rest in Shavasana afterwards.

steps.title: Who should modify or avoid
steps.body: Consult a doctor first if you have **high blood pressure, heart disease, back or disc problems, hernia, wrist or shoulder injuries**, are **pregnant**, or have had recent surgery. People with high blood pressure should move slowly and avoid head-down positions held for long. Fast, many-round 'challenges' are not suitable for beginners.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Do one slow round speaking the name of each position aloud. Then do it again in silence, focusing only on breathing with each movement.

activity.prompt: Put the first half of Surya Namaskar in order.
items: Pranamasana — prayer pose
Hasta Uttanasana — raised arms
Padahastasana — standing forward bend
Ashwa Sanchalanasana — lunge, one leg back
Parvatasana — mountain (inverted V)
Ashtanga Namaskara — knees, chest, chin to the floor
Bhujangasana — cobra

quiz.q: How many positions in the commonly taught Surya Namaskar?
quiz.why: The commonly taught Surya Namaskar has 12 positions in one half-round. A full round does the sequence on both sides.

quiz.q: Which position follows Ashtanga Namaskara?
quiz.why: After Ashtanga Namaskara (the eight-limbed salute), the next position is Bhujangasana (cobra).

quiz.q: How many rounds should a beginner start with?
quiz.why: A beginner should start with 2–3 slow rounds and build up gradually. 108 or 50 rounds would be too much.

quiz.q: Who should consult a doctor before Surya Namaskar?
options: People with high blood pressure, heart disease, back problems or pregnancy
quiz.why: People with high blood pressure, heart disease, back problems or pregnancy should consult a doctor first. These conditions may need modifications.

questions.q: International Day of Yoga is on…
questions.why: International Day of Yoga is on 21 June. 26 January is Republic Day in India.

questions.q: Shavasana is a…
questions.why: Shavasana (corpse pose) is the lying-down relaxation pose at the end of practice.

questions.q: Pain in a pose means…
questions.why: Pain is a warning, so ease off or stop. Pushing harder can cause injury.

questions.q: Vrikshasana is…
questions.why: Vrikshasana is the tree pose, a one-legged balancing pose. Cobra is Bhujangasana.

questions.q: Pranayama means…
questions.why: Pranayama means breath regulation. Asana is the word for posture.

questions.q: Which pose is a resting fold?
questions.why: Balasana (child's pose) is a resting forward fold. Trikonasana is an active standing pose.

questions.q: In Warrior II, the front knee…
questions.why: In Warrior II, the front knee tracks over the ankle. Letting it collapse inward strains the knee.

questions.q: Paschimottanasana should be approached carefully by…
questions.why: Paschimottanasana is a deep forward bend, so people with disc problems should be careful. Deep spinal flexion can aggravate a disc.

questions.q: Which limb is concentration?
questions.why: Dharana, concentration, is the sixth limb of yoga. Yama is the first limb, ethical restraints.

questions.q: Patanjali's Sutra 1.2 defines yoga as…
options: Stilling the fluctuations of the mind
questions.why: Patanjali's Yoga Sutra 1.2 says yoga is stilling the fluctuations of the mind (chitta vritti nirodhah). It is not about touching toes.

questions.q: Position 5 in the common Surya Namaskar sequence is…
questions.why: In the common 12-step sequence, position 5 is Parvatasana (mountain pose, a downward-facing V). Some versions use plank here.

questions.q: Someone with uncontrolled high blood pressure should avoid…
options: Long-held head-down positions and strong breath-holding
questions.why: With uncontrolled high blood pressure, avoid long-held head-down positions and strong breath-holding, as they can raise blood pressure. Gentle breathing is fine.

questions.q: Which publishes the Common Yoga Protocol?
questions.why: The Common Yoga Protocol is published by the Ministry of Ayush, India. The BCCI runs cricket.

courses.summary: How breathing works, diaphragmatic breathing, Nadi Shodhana, Bhramari, Kapalabhati with its important cautions, and relaxation for sleep, exams and competition.

lessons.title: Breathing basics: the diaphragm and slow breathing

scenes.text: Sanya, 15, in Delhi, freezes before her Class 10 mock exams — her heart races.
Her school counsellor teaches her belly breathing: hand on the belly, slow breath out longer than in.
She uses it for one minute before each paper.
'My hands still shake a bit,' she says, 'but my mind clears.'

steps.title: How breathing works
steps.body:
The **diaphragm** is a dome-shaped muscle under the lungs. When it contracts, it moves down, the belly gently moves out and air flows in. When it relaxes, air flows out.

Under stress many people breathe **fast and high in the chest**. Slow, low breathing — especially with a **longer out-breath** — tends to activate the body's calming (parasympathetic) response and lower heart rate.

steps.title: Diaphragmatic (belly) breathing
steps.body:
1. Sit tall or lie on your back, knees bent.
2. One hand on the chest, one on the belly.
3. Breathe in through the nose for about **4 counts** — the **belly hand rises**, the chest hand stays mostly still.
4. Breathe out gently through the nose or pursed lips for about **6 counts**.
5. Repeat for 1–5 minutes.

Never strain; if you feel light-headed, return to normal breathing.

steps.title: Where to use it
steps.body:
- Before an exam, a performance, a penalty kick, a serve.
- When you can't sleep.
- During a disagreement, before you reply.
- After intense exercise, to recover.

If anxiety is frequent and affects daily life, talk to a counsellor or doctor; **Tele-MANAS (14416)** offers free support in India.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forcing big, deep breaths (can cause dizziness).
- Lifting the shoulders to breathe.
- Expecting instant results — practise daily when calm so it works when stressed.

activity.label: Belly breathing: in for 4, out for 6. Hand on the belly.

quiz.q: Which muscle is the main breathing muscle?
quiz.why: The diaphragm, a dome-shaped muscle under the lungs, is the main breathing muscle. The heart is not a breathing muscle.

quiz.q: A longer out-breath tends to…
quiz.why: A longer out-breath tends to calm you, because it activates the body's calming (parasympathetic) response. A fast, shallow breath does the opposite.

quiz.q: In belly breathing, which hand should move most?
quiz.why: In belly breathing the belly hand moves most. The diaphragm moves down as you breathe in, pushing the belly out, while the chest stays fairly still.

quiz.q: Feeling light-headed means…
quiz.why: If you feel light-headed, go back to normal breathing. Forcing the breath or holding it can make it worse. Rest, and get up slowly.

lessons.title: Nadi Shodhana and Bhramari

scenes.text: Rohit, 17, a goalkeeper in Pune, gets so anxious before penalty shoot-outs that he can't think.
His coach, who also teaches yoga, shows him Bhramari — the humming-bee breath.
Rohit practises in the dressing room, hums quietly for five rounds.
In the next shoot-out, he feels calm and saves two penalties.

steps.title: Nadi Shodhana / Anulom Vilom (alternate-nostril breathing)
steps.body:
1. Sit comfortably, spine tall.
2. Right hand: fold the index and middle fingers in (Vishnu mudra) or rest them on the forehead; use the **thumb** to close the right nostril and the **ring finger** to close the left.
3. Close the right nostril; **inhale through the left**.
4. Close the left; open the right; **exhale through the right**.
5. **Inhale through the right**; close it; **exhale through the left**. That's one round.
6. Do 5–10 rounds, slowly and without strain. Beginners don't hold the breath.

Skip it if your nose is blocked.

steps.title: Bhramari (humming-bee breath)
steps.body:
1. Sit comfortably, eyes closed.
2. Optionally, gently close the ears with the thumbs or index fingers (on the cartilage flap, not inside the ear).
3. Inhale through the nose.
4. Exhale slowly making a steady **'mmmm' humming sound**, like a bee, mouth closed.
5. Feel the vibration in the head; repeat 5–7 times.

Many find it calming before sleep or performance.

steps.title: Cautions
steps.body:
- Avoid Bhramari lying down, and avoid pressing into the ears if you have an ear infection.
- Stop any practice if you feel dizzy or anxious.
- People with heart or lung conditions should keep the breath easy and natural and consult their doctor before breath-retention techniques.

activity.prompt: Order one round of Nadi Shodhana.
items: Close the right nostril with the thumb
Inhale through the left nostril
Close the left nostril with the ring finger and release the right
Exhale through the right nostril
Inhale through the right nostril
Close the right, release the left, and exhale through the left

quiz.q: In Nadi Shodhana, which finger usually closes the left nostril (right hand)?
quiz.why: In Nadi Shodhana with the right hand, the thumb closes the right nostril and the ring finger closes the left nostril. You switch between them as you breathe.

quiz.q: Bhramari involves…
options: A humming sound on the exhale
quiz.why: Bhramari, the humming-bee breath, involves a humming sound as you breathe out. It is calming.

quiz.q: Should beginners hold their breath in Nadi Shodhana?
quiz.why: Beginners should not hold their breath in Nadi Shodhana. Breath retention is an advanced practice, so breathe smoothly without holding.

quiz.q: Bhramari should be avoided…
options: Lying down, and with ear infections pressing on the ears
quiz.why: Bhramari should not be done lying down, and should not be done with pressure on the ears if there is an ear infection. Sitting practice is the usual way.

lessons.title: Kapalabhati and forceful techniques: who must avoid them

scenes.text: Mrs. Rao, 60, from Visakhapatnam, sees a TV programme promoting 15 minutes of Kapalabhati daily.
She has high blood pressure and a hernia operation last year.
Her daughter suggests asking her doctor first. The doctor advises gentle breathing instead.
Mrs. Rao does Nadi Shodhana and Bhramari daily and feels great — safely.

steps.title: What Kapalabhati is
steps.body: Kapalabhati ('skull-shining breath') is a **forceful, rapid exhalation** produced by sharply pulling the belly in, followed by a **passive** inhalation. It's an energising, cleansing practice traditionally described as a kriya (cleansing technique).

steps.title: How it's done (only if healthy)
steps.body:
1. Sit tall, hands on knees.
2. Take a normal breath in.
3. Exhale sharply through the nose by pulling the belly in; let the inhale happen by itself.
4. Start with **one round of 10–20 strokes**, slowly (about 1 per second), then breathe normally.
5. Increase gradually over weeks. Stop if light-headed.

Best learned from a qualified teacher.

steps.title: Who should avoid Kapalabhati
steps.body:
Avoid (or only with a doctor's permission) if you have:

- **High blood pressure or heart disease**
- **Pregnancy**, or during menstruation if it causes discomfort
- **Hernia** or recent abdominal or chest surgery
- **Epilepsy**
- **Glaucoma** or recent eye surgery
- **Acute asthma** or other lung problems, a nosebleed tendency, or a cold/blocked nose

Rapid breathing can also make some people dizzy or anxious. Children should do only gentle breathing techniques.

steps.title: Be careful with big health claims
steps.body: Pranayama can help relaxation and breathing awareness, and research suggests slow breathing practices may help stress and blood pressure in some people. But **no breathing technique cures diabetes, cancer, heart disease or other serious illnesses**. Never stop prescribed medicine because of a breathing practice.

activity.prompt: Kapalabhati: who should avoid it (or get medical advice first)?
buckets: Usually OK for a healthy adult learning with a teacher

items.text: Healthy 25-year-old athlete starting with 10 slow strokes

quiz.q: In Kapalabhati, the exhalation is…
quiz.why: In Kapalabhati the exhalation is forceful, with a quick belly contraction. The inhalation that follows is passive.

quiz.q: Which person should avoid Kapalabhati without medical advice?
quiz.why: Someone with high blood pressure should avoid Kapalabhati without medical advice, because the forceful breathing can raise blood pressure.

quiz.q: Can a breathing technique replace prescribed medicine?
quiz.why: A breathing technique cannot replace prescribed medicine. Never stop prescribed treatment without your doctor's advice.

quiz.q: How should a healthy beginner start?
quiz.why: A healthy beginner should start with one slow round of 10–20 strokes and build up gradually. 500 strokes or 15 minutes non-stop is too much.

lessons.title: Relaxation for sleep, exams and competition

scenes.text: Lakshmi, 19, a badminton player in Hyderabad, can't sleep the night before a state final.
She keeps checking her phone, which makes it worse.
She puts the phone away, does a body-scan relaxation and box breathing.
She sleeps, plays well, and decides to make the routine a habit.

steps.title: Box breathing
steps.body: In 4 – hold 4 – out 4 – hold 4. Used by many athletes and people in high-pressure jobs to steady themselves. Do 4–6 rounds. If holds feel uncomfortable, shorten them or skip them.

steps.title: Progressive muscle relaxation and body scan
steps.body:
- **Progressive muscle relaxation**: tense a muscle group gently for 5 seconds (e.g., fists), then release for 10–15 seconds, noticing the difference. Move from feet to face.
- **Body scan / Yoga Nidra-style**: lie in Shavasana and move your attention slowly through each body part, simply noticing and softening.

steps.title: Sleep habits for active people
steps.body:
- Teenagers generally need **8–10 hours**, adults **7–9 hours**.
- Same sleep and wake time daily.
- Screens off 30–60 minutes before bed; keep the room dark and cool.
- Avoid caffeine (tea, coffee, energy drinks, cola) late in the day.
- A light snack is fine; avoid heavy meals right before bed.

steps.title: A pre-competition routine
steps.body:
1. Arrive early; familiar warm-up.
2. 1–2 minutes of slow breathing (longer out-breath).
3. A cue word ('Ready', 'Smooth').
4. Picture your first action going well.
5. Accept nerves as normal — 'this is energy'.

activity.label: Box breathing: in 4, hold 4, out 4, hold 4.

quiz.q: Box breathing pattern is…
quiz.why: Box breathing has four equal parts, 4-4-4-4: breathe in for 4, hold for 4, breathe out for 4, hold for 4. The 'box' has four equal sides.

quiz.q: Progressive muscle relaxation involves…
quiz.why: Progressive muscle relaxation means tensing a muscle group and then releasing it, moving through the body. The contrast helps you notice relaxation.

quiz.q: How much sleep do teenagers generally need?
quiz.why: Teenagers generally need 8–10 hours of sleep. Less than this affects mood, learning and recovery.

quiz.q: A sensible pre-sleep habit is…
quiz.why: Switching screens off 30–60 minutes before bed helps sleep. Screen light and stimulation delay sleep, and energy drinks, hard exercise or a heavy late meal also hurt it.

questions.q: Main breathing muscle?
questions.why: The diaphragm is the main breathing muscle. The triceps is an arm muscle.

questions.q: Bhramari makes which sound?
questions.why: Bhramari makes a humming sound, like a bee, on the exhale.

questions.q: Box breathing has how many equal parts?
questions.why: Box breathing has 4 equal parts: breathe in, hold, breathe out, hold.

questions.q: A longer exhale tends to…
questions.why: A longer exhale tends to calm the body by engaging its calming (parasympathetic) response. It does not speed up the heart.

questions.q: Alternate-nostril breathing is called…
questions.why: Alternate-nostril breathing is Nadi Shodhana (also called Anulom Vilom). Kapalabhati is a forceful exhale breath.

questions.q: Teen sleep need?
questions.why: Teenagers need about 8–10 hours of sleep. 4–5 hours is too little.

questions.q: Kapalabhati exhalation is…
questions.why: In Kapalabhati the exhale is forceful and the inhale passive.

questions.q: Who should avoid Kapalabhati without medical advice?
options: Pregnant women and people with hypertension
questions.why: Pregnant women and people with hypertension should avoid Kapalabhati without medical advice. The forceful breathing affects pressure in the abdomen and blood pressure.

questions.q: In belly breathing, which moves most?
questions.why: In belly breathing, the belly moves most, because the diaphragm drives it. The shoulders should stay relaxed.

questions.q: Can pranayama cure diabetes?
options: No — it can support wellbeing but doesn't cure disease
questions.why: Pranayama can support wellbeing, but it does not cure diabetes or other diseases. Claims of a cure are exaggerated.

questions.q: Progressive muscle relaxation works by…
questions.why: Progressive muscle relaxation works by tensing a muscle and then releasing it. The contrast makes the relaxed feeling clearer.

questions.q: Why practise breathing techniques when calm?
options: So they become automatic under stress
questions.why: Practise breathing techniques when you are calm so they become automatic. Then you can use them under stress. Skills learned in calm times carry over to pressure.

questions.q: Beginners in Nadi Shodhana should…
questions.why: Beginners should skip breath retention in Nadi Shodhana. Holding the breath is advanced and can cause dizziness.

courses.title: Sports nutrition and hydration: eat to play, myths busted
courses.summary: Macronutrients and the balanced Indian plate, how much protein and carbohydrate active people need, iron and anaemia, hydration and ORS, what to eat before, during and after training, and the supplements, doping and diet myths to avoid.
outcomes: Learners can explain carbohydrates, protein, fat and their energy values
Learners can estimate protein needs and build a vegetarian or non-vegetarian sports plate
Learners can plan hydration and recognise dehydration and over-drinking
Learners can time meals around training
Learners can spot common nutrition myths and supplement risks, including doping

lessons.title: Macronutrients and the balanced Indian plate

scenes.text: Ravi, 17, a kabaddi player from Rohtak, cuts out roti and rice because a gym video said 'carbs are bad'.
Within two weeks he's exhausted in training and irritable.
His coach sends him to the team dietitian, who explains that carbohydrates are an athlete's main fuel.
With rice, roti, dal, curd, vegetables and fruit back on his plate, his energy returns.

steps.title: The three macronutrients
steps.body:
- **Carbohydrates** — **4 kcal per gram**. The main fuel for high-intensity exercise and the brain. Sources: rice, roti, millets (ragi, jowar, bajra), oats, poha, potatoes, fruit, milk.
- **Protein** — **4 kcal per gram**. Builds and repairs muscles, enzymes and immune cells. Sources: dal, rajma, chana, soy, paneer, curd, milk, eggs, fish, chicken, nuts and seeds.
- **Fat** — **9 kcal per gram**. Energy for longer, lower-intensity activity, hormones, absorbing vitamins A, D, E, K. Sources: oils, ghee, nuts, seeds, fish.

**Micronutrients** (vitamins and minerals), **fibre** and **water** are essential too.

steps.title: Building a balanced plate
steps.body:
The ICMR–NIN *Dietary Guidelines for Indians* (2024) promote a varied plate built from **vegetables and fruits, whole grains or millets, pulses/eggs/fish/meat, milk or curd, and nuts and seeds**, and recommend **limiting salt, sugar and ultra-processed foods**.

A simple visual for each main meal:
- **Half** the plate: vegetables and fruit (including greens).
- **Quarter**: grains — rice, roti, millets.
- **Quarter**: protein — dal, paneer, eggs, fish, chicken, soy.
- Plus curd or milk, and a little healthy fat.

steps.title: Salt and sugar
steps.body: WHO recommends **less than 5 g of salt a day** (about a teaspoon) for adults, and keeping **free sugars below 10%** of daily energy, ideally below 5%. Pickles, papad, namkeen, instant noodles and packaged snacks are often high in salt; soft drinks and sweets are high in sugar.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Cutting out a whole food group because of social-media advice.
- Skipping breakfast before morning training.
- Relying on packaged 'health' bars and drinks.
- Under-eating — athletes who don't eat enough for their training can develop **RED-S** (relative energy deficiency in sport): fatigue, frequent injuries, missed periods in girls and women, weaker bones. Talk to a doctor if you notice these signs.

activity.prompt: Sort the foods by their main macronutrient.

items.text: Paneer and dal (both rich in protein)

quiz.q: How many kcal does 1 g of fat provide?
quiz.why: Fat gives 9 kcal per gram. Carbohydrate and protein give about 4 kcal per gram.

quiz.q: The main fuel for high-intensity exercise is…
quiz.why: Carbohydrate is the main fuel for high-intensity exercise. Muscles use stored carbohydrate (glycogen) quickly. Water and vitamins do not give energy.

quiz.q: WHO recommends adult salt intake below…
quiz.why: WHO recommends adults take less than 5 g of salt a day. Higher intakes raise the risk of high blood pressure.

quiz.q: Which is a sign of RED-S?
quiz.why: Missed periods and frequent injuries are signs of RED-S (relative energy deficiency in sport). Low energy intake harms hormones and bones. If this is noticed, a doctor should be seen.

quiz.q: On the plate visual, half the plate is…
quiz.why: On the plate visual, half the plate is vegetables and fruit. The rest is split between whole grains and protein foods.

lessons.title: Protein and carbohydrate needs (with vegetarian plans)

scenes.text: Gurpreet, 19, a wrestler from Punjab, is vegetarian. Friends say he 'can't get enough protein'.
His dietitian calculates his needs from his body weight and training.
His plan: milk, curd, paneer, dal, chana, soy chunks, peanuts — spread over the day.
He meets his target without any supplement and gains strength steadily.

steps.title: How much protein?
steps.body:
- **General adults**: ICMR–NIN (2020) sets the recommended dietary allowance at about **0.83 g per kg body weight per day**.
- **Active people and athletes**: sports nutrition position statements (e.g., ACSM and partners, 2016) suggest about **1.2–2.0 g/kg/day**, depending on training.
- **Spread it out**: roughly 0.25–0.3 g/kg per meal over 3–5 meals, including after training.

Most people meet their needs from food alone.

steps.title: Worked example: a 60 kg athlete
steps.body:
At 1.4 g/kg: 60 × 1.4 = **84 g protein/day**.

A vegetarian day (approximate values):
- 2 glasses milk (500 ml) ≈ 16 g
- 1 bowl curd (200 g) ≈ 7 g
- 100 g paneer ≈ 18 g
- 2 bowls dal (cooked) ≈ 14 g
- 1 bowl chana or rajma (cooked) ≈ 9 g
- 30 g soy chunks (dry weight) ≈ 15 g
- Handful of peanuts (30 g) ≈ 7 g
- Grains (roti, rice) through the day ≈ 10 g

Total ≈ **96 g** — target met. Values vary by brand and recipe; read labels.

steps.title: How much carbohydrate?
steps.body:
Carbohydrate needs rise with training:
- **Light training** (low intensity or skill-based): about **3–5 g/kg/day**.
- **Moderate** (about 1 hour a day): about **5–7 g/kg/day**.
- **High volume** (1–3 hours a day of moderate-to-high intensity): about **6–10 g/kg/day**.

These are from sports nutrition guidelines; individual needs vary.

steps.title: Plant protein tips
steps.body:
- **Combine** cereals and pulses (rice + dal, roti + rajma) — they complement each other's amino acids.
- Include **soy, milk products, peanuts** — rich, affordable sources.
- Vegans: tofu, soy, legumes, nuts, seeds; consider vitamin B12 (ask a doctor).

activity.prompt: A 70 kg athlete aims for 1.5 g of protein per kg per day. How many grams per day?

quiz.q: ICMR–NIN's adult protein RDA is about…
quiz.why: ICMR–NIN gives the adult protein RDA as about 0.83 g per kg of body weight a day. 3 or 5 g/kg is far too high.

quiz.q: Athletes often need about…
quiz.why: Athletes often need about 1.2–2.0 g of protein per kg a day, more than the general RDA. 5–10 g/kg is the carbohydrate range, not protein.

quiz.q: Can vegetarians meet protein needs from food?
options: Yes, with milk, curd, paneer, pulses, soy and nuts
quiz.why: Vegetarians can meet protein needs from milk, curd, paneer, pulses, soy and nuts. Eggs or supplements are not needed.

quiz.q: For high-volume training, carbohydrate needs are about…
quiz.why: For high-volume training, carbohydrate needs are about 6–10 g/kg a day. More training means more fuel is needed.

quiz.q: Why combine rice with dal?
options: They complement each other's amino acids
quiz.why: Rice and dal complement each other's amino acids. Cereals are low in some amino acids that pulses supply, and the reverse, so together they give better-quality protein.

sources: ACSM/AND/DC position on nutrition and athletic performance (2016)

lessons.title: Hydration, ORS and electrolytes

scenes.text: Sneha, 32, runs her first half-marathon in humid Mumbai.
Her friend Ankit drinks litre after litre of plain water at every station, worried about dehydration.
Near the end Ankit feels confused, nauseous and bloated — medics suspect low blood sodium from over-drinking.
He recovers in the medical tent. Sneha, who drank to thirst and took some electrolytes, finishes strong.

steps.title: Why hydration matters
steps.body: Water regulates body temperature, carries nutrients and keeps blood flowing to muscles. Losing more than about **2% of body weight** as sweat can impair performance, especially in heat. Sweat also contains **sodium** (salt), which must be replaced in long, sweaty sessions.

steps.title: A practical plan
steps.body:
- **Before**: drink regularly through the day; pale-yellow urine is a rough guide.
- **During** (sessions over ~60 minutes or in heat): drink to a plan or to thirst — small, regular sips. Include sodium/electrolytes in long sessions.
- **After**: replace losses — weigh yourself before and after; for each **1 kg lost**, gradually drink about **1.25–1.5 litres** of fluid along with salty food or electrolytes.
- Buttermilk (chaas) with a pinch of salt, nimbu pani with a little salt and sugar, coconut water and ORS are useful Indian options.

steps.title: ORS: the life-saving mix
steps.body:
**Oral rehydration solution (ORS)**, recommended by WHO, contains a precise balance of salts and glucose that helps the gut absorb water. Packaged WHO-formula ORS sachets are cheap and widely available in India — mix exactly as the packet says with clean water.

ORS is also the key treatment for dehydration from diarrhoea. 'Electrolyte drinks' sold as juices often have much more sugar and are not the same as ORS — check the label.

steps.title: Too little, too much
steps.body:
- **Dehydration** signs: thirst, dark urine, headache, dizziness, tiredness, cramps.
- **Over-drinking** plain water during long events can dilute blood sodium (**hyponatraemia**) — headache, nausea, bloating, confusion, even seizures. It's a medical emergency (**112**). Don't drink far beyond thirst; don't gain weight during an event.
- Heat stroke (confusion, collapse with high body temperature) → call **112** and cool rapidly.

a.text: You're running a 2-hour event on a hot day. Which hydration plan is best?

choices.label: Drink a full litre at every water station regardless of thirst
choices.feedback: Over-drinking can cause hyponatraemia.

choices.label: Sip regularly to thirst and take electrolytes/ORS for sodium
choices.feedback: Balanced and safe.

b.text: At 90 minutes you feel bloated, nauseous and have a headache. What do you do?

choices.label: Stop drinking plain water, go to the medical tent and tell them how much you drank
choices.feedback: Right — possible low sodium needs medical care.

c.text: After the race you've lost 1.2 kg. How much fluid should you gradually drink?

choices.label: About 1.5–1.8 litres over the next hours, with salty food
choices.feedback: About 1.25–1.5 L per kg lost.

choices.label: Nothing — weight loss is fat loss
choices.feedback: Short-term weight loss in exercise is mostly fluid.

end1.text: Perfect recovery plan. You'll feel much better tomorrow.

end2.text: Getting help was right. Next time drink to thirst and include sodium.

end3.text: Sweat loss is water, not fat. Rehydrate gradually after exercise.

quiz.q: Losing more than about what percent of body weight in sweat can impair performance?
quiz.why: Losing about 2% or more of body weight in sweat can impair performance. This is why staying hydrated matters.

quiz.q: For each 1 kg lost in exercise, drink about…
quiz.why: For each 1 kg lost, drink about 1.25–1.5 litres (125–150% of the loss) over time. This replaces ongoing losses as well.

quiz.q: Drinking far too much plain water in long events can cause…
quiz.why: Drinking far too much plain water in long events can dilute blood sodium, causing hyponatraemia. It does not build muscle or speed.

quiz.q: How should packaged ORS be prepared?
options: Exactly as the packet says with clean water
quiz.why: Prepare packaged ORS exactly as the packet says, with clean water. The correct concentration matters, because too much or too little works less well.

quiz.q: Short-term weight lost during a sweaty session is mostly…
quiz.why: Weight lost in a short, sweaty session is mostly water. It is fluid that needs replacing, and not fat or muscle.

lessons.title: Eating around training: before, during and after

scenes.text: Aditi, 14, from Bengaluru, swims at 6 a.m. on an empty stomach and feels dizzy by 7.
Her coach suggests a banana and a glass of milk 30–60 minutes before.
After practice, she has idli-sambar or a paneer sandwich within an hour or two.
Her training quality improves and she stops feeling faint.

steps.title: Before training
steps.body:
- **3–4 hours before**: a normal balanced meal — e.g., rice, dal, vegetables, curd.
- **1–2 hours before**: a lighter, carb-rich snack — poha, upma, idli, a sandwich, fruit with curd.
- **30–60 minutes before**: something small and easy to digest — a banana, dates, a glass of milk, a few biscuits.
- Avoid very fatty, spicy or high-fibre foods right before if they upset your stomach. **Test new foods in training, never on match day.**

steps.title: During training
steps.body:
- Under ~60 minutes: water is usually enough.
- **Longer than 60–90 minutes**: about **30–60 g of carbohydrate per hour** (e.g., a banana ≈ 25 g, a few dates, a sports drink) plus fluid and sodium. For very long events (over 2.5 hours) some athletes trained to it use up to about 90 g/hour.

steps.title: After training
steps.body:
Within a couple of hours, have a meal or snack with **carbohydrate + protein**:
- Milk or lassi with a banana.
- Curd rice with dal.
- Egg or paneer roll.
- Chana chaat.
- Idli-sambar.

About **20–40 g of protein** after training supports muscle repair; carbohydrate refuels.

steps.title: Match day tips
steps.body:
- Eat familiar foods.
- Pack snacks and water — don't rely on venue food.
- Avoid trying a new supplement or energy drink on match day.
- Energy drinks with lots of caffeine are **not recommended for children and teens**.

activity.prompt: Order these by time, from earliest before training to after.

Sips of water; carbs if over 60–90 min

quiz.q: A good snack 30–60 minutes before training is…
quiz.why: A banana is easy-to-digest carbohydrate that gives energy before training. Fried pakoras or a large biryani are heavy and may cause stomach upset.

quiz.q: For sessions over 60–90 minutes, aim for about…
quiz.why: For sessions over 60–90 minutes, aim for about 30–60 g of carbohydrate per hour. This keeps the fuel supply going.

quiz.q: Recovery meals should combine…
quiz.why: Recovery meals should combine carbohydrate to refuel and protein to repair muscle. Only sweets, fat or water would not do both.

quiz.q: When should you test new foods?
quiz.why: Test new foods in training. This avoids surprises like stomach upset on competition day.

lessons.title: Myths, supplements and doping risks

scenes.text: Kabir, 20, a sprinter from Lucknow, buys an online 'herbal muscle booster' promising fast gains.
At a national event, his dope test comes back positive for a banned steroid that was hidden in the product.
Under strict liability, he is responsible for what's in his body — he's banned.
He now speaks to young athletes: 'Food first. Ask before you take anything.'

steps.title: Myths, busted
steps.body:
- **'Spot reduction'** (crunches burn belly fat): **false** — fat loss happens across the body with an energy deficit.
- **'Sweating a lot = losing fat'**: **false** — it's water.
- **'Carbs make you fat'**: excess total energy causes fat gain, not carbohydrate itself. Active people need carbs.
- **'You need protein shakes to build muscle'**: **false** — food can provide enough; shakes are just convenient.
- **'Eating after 8 pm makes you fat'**: total daily intake matters more than the clock (though late heavy meals can disturb sleep).
- **'Detox teas cleanse the body'**: the liver and kidneys do that; many detox products are just laxatives or diuretics.
- **'More protein is always better'**: beyond needs, extra protein is simply used for energy.

steps.title: Iron and anaemia
steps.body:
Anaemia is very common in India — **more than half of adolescent girls** were anaemic in NFHS-5 (2019–21). Athletes, especially girls and women, are at risk because of growth, menstruation and sweat losses.

- Iron sources: green leafy vegetables, legumes, jaggery-containing foods (small amounts), ragi, eggs, meat, fish.
- **Vitamin C** (amla, lemon, guava, oranges) with meals boosts iron absorption.
- **Tea or coffee with meals** reduces absorption — have them between meals.
- Persistent tiredness or breathlessness → get a blood test; don't self-prescribe iron tablets.

steps.title: Supplements and doping
steps.body:
- Supplements are **not tightly regulated** in many countries; studies have found some products **contaminated** with banned substances not on the label.
- Under the **strict liability** principle of the World Anti-Doping Code, **athletes are responsible for any prohibited substance found in their body**, whatever the source.
- India's **National Anti Doping Agency (NADA)** runs testing and education. Check the current **WADA Prohibited List** and ask your team doctor before taking any medicine or supplement.
- **Never** take steroids or 'injections for strength' — serious health harm and bans.
- Teens: food first; supplements only on medical advice (e.g., diagnosed deficiency).

steps.title: How to judge a nutrition claim
steps.body:
- Who's selling it? Do they profit from it?
- Does it promise fast, dramatic results? Red flag.
- Is there good research (not just testimonials)?
- What do a registered dietitian or doctor say?

When in doubt: **food first, sleep well, train smart**.

statements.s: Crunches burn fat specifically from the belly.
statements.why: Spot reduction doesn't work.

statements.s: Athletes are responsible for any banned substance found in their body, even from a contaminated supplement.
statements.why: Strict liability under the World Anti-Doping Code.

statements.s: Having tea with meals improves iron absorption.
statements.why: Tea reduces it; vitamin C improves it.

statements.s: Most people can meet protein needs from food.
statements.why: Supplements are convenience, not necessity.

statements.s: Weight lost by sweating in a sauna is fat loss.
statements.why: It's water and comes back when you drink.

statements.s: Detox teas are needed because the liver can't clean the body.
statements.why: The liver and kidneys handle detoxification.

quiz.q: Which agency runs anti-doping in India?
quiz.why: NADA, the National Anti Doping Agency, runs anti-doping in India. The BCCI and AIFF govern sports, not doping tests.

quiz.q: 'Strict liability' means…
options: You're responsible for any banned substance in your body
quiz.why: Strict liability means you are responsible for any banned substance found in your body, whatever the reason. The athlete cannot blame a coach or a supplement.

quiz.q: Which helps iron absorption?
quiz.why: Vitamin C foods with meals help the body absorb non-haem (plant) iron. Tea and coffee reduce iron absorption.

quiz.q: Fat loss happens mainly through…
options: An overall energy deficit over time
quiz.why: Fat loss happens through an overall energy deficit over time. Spot exercises, sweating and detox teas do not target fat.

quiz.q: A product promises 10 kg of muscle in a month. This is…
quiz.why: A promise of 10 kg of muscle in a month is a red flag. Real muscle gain is slow, so such claims signal a scam or a dangerous product.

questions.q: Carbohydrate provides how many kcal per gram?
questions.why: Carbohydrate gives 4 kcal per gram. Fat gives 9.

questions.q: Which is a good post-training snack?
questions.why: Milk with a banana gives carbohydrate and protein, which helps recovery. Cola alone gives only sugar.

questions.q: Sweat loss during exercise is mostly…
questions.why: Weight lost in exercise is mostly water lost as sweat, not fat.

questions.q: Fat provides how many kcal per gram?
questions.why: Fat gives 9 kcal per gram, more than double the 4 kcal of carbohydrate.

questions.q: Packaged ORS should be mixed…
options: Exactly as directed with clean water
questions.why: Mix packaged ORS exactly as directed, with clean water. The right concentration helps the body absorb it.

questions.q: Which helps iron absorption?
questions.why: Amla or lemon with meals provides vitamin C, which helps absorb iron from plant foods. Tea reduces absorption.

questions.q: Athlete protein range per sports guidelines?
questions.why: Athletes usually need about 1.2–2.0 g of protein per kg a day. 0.1–0.3 g/kg is far too little.

questions.q: 60 kg athlete at 1.5 g/kg protein needs…
questions.why: Protein need = body weight × g/kg = 60 × 1.5 = 90 g a day.

questions.q: Over-drinking plain water in a marathon can cause…
questions.why: Drinking too much plain water in a marathon can dilute blood sodium, which is called hyponatraemia. Hypertrophy is muscle growth.

questions.q: A runner loses 2 kg in training. Fluid to drink gradually afterwards?
questions.why: Drink about 1.25–1.5 L per kg lost. For 2 kg that is 2.5–3 L, taken gradually.

questions.q: RED-S stands for…
questions.why: RED-S stands for relative energy deficiency in sport. It happens when energy intake is too low for the energy used, which harms health and performance.

questions.q: For a 90-minute+ session, carbohydrate intake during exercise of about…
questions.why: During 90 minutes or more of exercise, about 30–60 g of carbohydrate per hour is the standard guidance. 300 g/hour is far more than the gut can absorb.

questions.q: An athlete tests positive from a contaminated supplement. Under the World Anti-Doping Code…
options: The athlete is still responsible (strict liability)
questions.why: Under strict liability, an athlete is responsible for what is in their body, even from a contaminated supplement. Fault may affect the sanction, but not the responsibility.

questions.q: ICMR–NIN adult protein RDA (2020) is about…
questions.why: The ICMR–NIN 2020 adult protein RDA is about 0.83 g per kg per day. 2.5 g/kg is much more than needed by most adults.
